How it burned physical materials when focused and outright vaporized Gloam it came into touch with. He explained it all until he was left to pant.

“Izel is telling us this,” Song spoke into the silence that followed, “because I pressed him to take his lenslight and install it on the skimmer so we might field it against the ketos.”

She had not said it with guilt, he thought, but like someone taking responsibility. Like an officer. He could respect that more than feigned regret for something she still wanted to happen.

“And I don’t want to,” Izel said, passing a hand through his stubble, “because if I do use it, within a decade someone will have used a lenslight to set fire to a city.”

Across much of Vesper, roofs were still thatched. For the price of a pair of cannons, a clever tinker could make a lenslight-like machine that would set a thatched roof on fire from a mile away on a clear night – assuming the scaling held up. The bottleneck would be getting aether-forged glass lenses of the right size, but their current rarity was not because the means to make such pieces did not exist. It was because no one really had a use for such large lenses.

“I left Izcalli in no small part because I did not want to make weapons for my father,” Izel admitted. “I struggle with the notion of joining the Watch to make weapons anyhow.”

Maryam stirred in her seat again.

“No one else has been asked to cross their lines in the sand over this mess,” she said, eyeing Song. “It’s not right to ask it of you, any more than we would ask Angharad to break her word or myself to turn on my countrymen.”

“I don’t say this to shame Song out of the request,” Izel hastily said.

He licked his lips.

“I- I’d like your help,” Izel said. “I’m asking for it.”

“I am not sure how I can help you,” Angharad slowly said, “but you can take my aid as a given.”

“What is it you’re asking, Izel?” Tristan plainly said.

“The design is mine for five years,” he blurted out. “After that it’s open to all tinkers. Before those years pass, I need to have made the lenslight into something that’s so much more useful outside the battlefield that it’d be a waste to use them on one.”

He wrung his hands.

“I’m going to need materials for my tests,” he said. ‘’Expensive things, or restricted. Some that aren’t even sold. And I’m going to need access to archives and other tinkers. Even if you can’t help me with the designs, you can all help me get to things and people who _can_.”

“That seems a reasonable enough request,” Song slowly said.

“It’s _too_ nice,” Maryam complained.

“You should charge a fee at least,” Hooks agreed.

“It is rare that I should be requested for my penmanship instead of my sword hand, but I can put you in touch with my uncle,” Angharad promised.

Only Tristan remained silent.

“There can’t be any guarantees for something like this,” he finally said.

“Tristan,” Angharad reproached, but the Sacromontan raised a hand to stall her.

“There’s no certainty you’ll succeed in your five years,” he told Izel. “Or that we can pull through on our end of the bargain, or that in a few years we’ll still be able or willing to. You’d still make the offer, knowing this?”

Izel looked down at his hands.

“What’s the point, if I don’t trust you?” he simply said.

The thief’s face spasmed, for an instant, before Tristan shook his head.

“Then you have my word, whatever that’s worth,” he said.

“Enough,” Izel told him, and somehow that seemed to make things worse.

There was an awkward silence after, no one quite sure what to say, so he took it on himself to break it.

“No to be crude,” Izel said, “but the current lenslight is too small to be entirely feasible as a weapon against the ketos. I will need to enlarge it, which will require gold.”

“How much?” Song asked.

“About twenty ramas for everything,” he said. “Aether-forged lenses are not inexpensive.”

“We can’t afford that,” she said.

“We’ll be able to.”

Eyes swiveled back to Tristan, whose still-hoarse voice and pale face inspired little trust – until one saw the eyes. The gray had gone cold.

“Should I ask?” Song said.

--

Picking the lock would have hinted at professional work. So instead Tristan picked up a cobblestone, wrapped it in cloth and smashed in the window of the Colored Arches. A restaurant that high-end always kept enough gold on hand to cover enough for expensive imports.

--

“Best that you don’t,” Tristan replied.

Song cleared her throat.

“We also need funds for a large dose of_ plousperi_,” she admitted. “It’s currently our only means of keeping the ketos from submerging after we hit it.”

--

The lock on the strongbox popped open with a smooth click. The sheath of ministry papers stood in the corner, the corners slightly crumpled. Tristan was going to take a massive loss on the sum when fencing paper money through the Chimerical but, hey, it was Cao’s emergency funds.

--

“Fortunately, I’m about to come into some money,” Tristan smoothly replied.

“Whose?” Izel couldn’t resist asking.

“Ours,” he said. “Anything else pressing?”

Maryam cleared her throat.

“If we are going to take the Orels into combat, I would like to arm them,” she admitted.

--

A minute into picking the lock he lost patience, put his pistol against the slit and pulled the trigger. Tristan kicked open the door of the Warfare supply shed and opened his bag to begin shoving in swords, muskets and pistols.

--

“I know where some spares can be found,” Tristan blandly said. “The utility of all this, of course, rests on there being a plan to kill that thing – or at least drive it off.”

“I have one,” Song said. “It is... risky, however.”

“Insane,” Maryam flatly said. “I still can’t believe you asked me that.”

“It will work,” Song said. “The trouble is that we are going to need a boarding crew for it.”

Angharad cleared her throat.

“Here I believe I can lend a hand,” she said. “How many do you need?”

“At least three besides you,” Song said.

“I will take care of it,” Angharad said.

“I can have the modified lenslight installed within three days of paying for the materials,” Izel volunteered.

“Then you’ll have the gold come morning,” Tristan evenly said.

Maryam sighed.

“I’ll talk the Orels, find out how many are willing to sail into combat.”

Song Ren smiled coldly.

“Then it is on me to find us ships.”

--

Blade rang against blade.

Angharad gave a step and broke the lock, baiting a cut, but Lindiwe declined to be baited. Instead she feinted high and the mirror-dancer struggled to position her wrist to block it, getting a flick at her face for it. She managed to pull back at the last moment, avoiding a cut on her cheek, but only narrowly. Angharad was just a hair too slow on the riposte, Lindiwe dancing out of the way and snorting as she casually tucked a strand of hair back behind her ear.

“Sloppy,” Lindiwe Sarru said. “You’re not used to the weight yet.”

“It is heavier than my usual,” Angharad admitted.

Izel had done beautiful work in replacing her saber’s edge with tomic alloy, but however light the Antediluvian metal was it still added weight. He’d compensated by adding a touch of steel to the pommel, which had maintained the balance but also left the blade slightly heavier than she preferred.

“It’s too heavy to be a proper dueling saber now,” Lindiwe said.

Angharad opened her mouth to object, but the other woman rolled her eyes.

“Yes, yes, I’m sure you can drill to compensate for it,” she said. “A few months of practice should mostly make up for the difference. But that’s avoiding the point, which is that Coyac turned your pretty saber into a very fine monster-killing blade.”

Lindiwe clicked her tongue in distaste.

“A little more weight lets you carve through hide properly and the tomic edge will let you cut even spirits,” she said. “It might not be mirror-dancer’s blade, but it is the blade of watchwoman.”

“One can be both, Lindiwe,” Angharad flatly replied.

“We can be all sorts of things,” Lindiwe agreed. “But there’s an order to the list of our allegiances, Tredegar. That blade puts Skiritai above duelist, which is a welcome change.”

Biting down on a dozen unkind answers, Angharad forced herself to let it go. There was no victory to be had in a philosophy debate. She took a step back instead, catching her breath.

“Thank you for the spar.”

“It’s only sensible to test your new tomic edge against a match,” Lindiwe said, tapping the side of her own saber. “I was curious how it would take to candlesteel myself, but they don’t seem to be reacting to each other at all.”

Angharad had been curious as well. Tomic alloy, the very wonder that allowed one to build skimmers, was said to ‘cut’ through both the aether and material realms in a way that allowed those wondrous ships to have nearly unparalleled speed at sea. Candlesteel, on the other hand, was not said to have any particular physical properties beyond being lighter than standard steel – it was famous because its mere proximity was disruptive to both aether and Gloam.

“There is a sense to it,” Angharad noted. “Candlesteel affects metaphysical forces, which tomic materials are not even though they affect them as well.”

“I don’t expect it’s been studied in detail,” Lindiwe dismissed. “Candlesteel is tightly restricted and tomic alloys so expensive I can’t recall hearing of another sword worked with it.”

Angharad ceded the point with a nod.

“How did you get such a blade, anyhow? If you don’t mind my asking.”

“My great-grandfather warred in Izcalli,” she proudly said. “He slew a Crocodile Society champion in single combat and claimed her weapon as a prize. There was just enough candlesteel in the spearhead to forge an alloyed blade.”

A family heirloom, then. Angharad was surprised it would be allowed into the hands of a scion headed into the Watch, but then she knew next to nothing of Lindiwe Sarru’s house.

“But we’re not here for you to paw at my family history, you Pereduri country mouse,” Lindiwe conversationally added. “You said you had an offer for me – what is it?”

Her smile turned barbed.

“You must be quite desperate to come begging to me for help after abandoning me to the Acallar hunts.”

Angharad watched her, jaw clenched, and saw that once more Lindiwe Sarru was tripping over her own pride. The same way she had at the table with Musa, Alizia and Tall Bibek when instead of trading for what she wanted she had made demands and antagonized all those whose help she wanted before spurning even Angharad’s attempt at reparations.

Lindiwe might not be wearing bandages on her head anymore, but Shalini had been clear that her hunting crew’s attempts on Steel list beasts had stalled. Her allies had taken too many wounds and the group she had cobbled together after the hunt and delve drew Skiritai away from the Acallar was not anywhere as tightly-knight and motivated as the one she had begun the year with.

If she kept pushing them, they would leave.

And still Angharad could see that Lindiwe had come here this morning mostly for the pleasure of refusing her. Of, the way she saw it, evening the score for earlier this year. Only Angharad had not come here to rope the Tenth Brigade in through an acquaintance, and she knew exactly how to pay for what she wanted.

“I want your help against the ketos,” she said.

Lindiwe smiled beatifically.

“No,” she said, and immediately began to walk away.

“Not your brigade,” Angharad said. “Yours.”

The steps stuttered, out of surprise, but did not stop.

“In exchange, I will join your hunting crew until your loss is redeemed,” she continued.

Lindiwe stopped. She turned around, face disbelieving.

“These exact terms?” she said.

Angharad did not grimace, though she felt like it. Lindiwe was fighting to revive the member of her hunting crew who had died last year, but the span of time for it was narrowing. The phrasing Angharad had given implied that should that opportunity pass, she would remain part of Lindiwe’s hunting crew as a subordinate. There was a natural cutoff there, as when they graduated Scholomance there would no longer be hunting crews and thus the promise came at an end, but it was still putting her remaining years here on the line.

“These exact terms,” she forced herself to reply.

Lindiwe let out a low whistle.

“You are more desperate than I thought,” Lindiwe said. “Or more impressed by me than you’re willing to admit. You’re willing to pay this much for myself alone?”

“For the plan my captain has put together to work, we need a Skiritai band to take the lead,” Angharad said.

At least four. Fewer than that and there would be gaps. Lindiwe’s brow rose.

“Who else do you have?”

“Shalini,” she said, then stalled.

“Salvador blew you off,” Lindiwe guessed with a sharp-toothed grin.

“He declined,” Angharad sharply corrected. “And I have other prospects, I simply came to you early.”

Lindiwe cocked her head to the side.

“Tall Bibek?”

Angharad kept her face blank, refusing to answer. Else she would have to admit he had already refused as well. The potential fourth was an... unexpected turn, but Izel had been firm.

“You say your captain has a plan?” Lindiwe probed.

“One I believe will work,” Angharad said.

The other woman worried her lip.

“It’s a pretty offer you make me,” Lindiwe admitted. “But I will not commit to putting my life on the line before hearing what bold folly the Thirteenth has cooked up this time.”

Angharad’s eyes narrowed at her. Lindiwe was angling to get to sit on the coming conversation without committing anything, and though Angharad badly needed the sword-arm she could not allow that. She pressed the other woman for an agreement-in-principle, the promise to go through with the deal under the current terms if the plan was acceptable, and though Lindiwe tried to wriggle out Angharad put her foot down and the other Skiritai had to consider whether blowing this up now was really what she wanted.

It was not.

It meant, unfortunately, that as Angharad began her trek to the Dregs she was accompanied by a smiling Lindiwe Sarru – whose irritation at having given her agreement-in-principle vanished into smoke around the first time someone pointed at Angharad. As Captain Wen had predicted, it’d gotten worse after news of Izel’s protection of Young Koval spread around town. Considering violence had been resorted to only in order to prevent the abduction of a child Angharad would have expected the people of Allazei to see the sense in it, but no.

All they saw was one body under a black sheet and two sent to Lady Knit’s mercy while the Unluckies went unpunished.

“I hear one of the fishmongers refused to sell to your brigade,” Lindiwe ‘idly’ said as they strode down the street.

“That is their right,” Angharad made herself reply.

The man had lost a brother in the fire and blamed them for it. Song had not deserved the scene he made, but the Khaimovs reacting by drawing Gloam had not helped – even if they never used it. Angharad heard the hard laugh from a corner as they turned west and forced herself not to look. She would rather not know if she was being pointed at.

“It’s actually eating you alive, isn’t?” Lindiwe said, her tone wondering.

“Is there anyone who enjoys having a poor reputation?” Angharad said sharply.

“No,” she replied, raising her hands in appeasement.

It might have worked better without the smirk tugging at her lips.

“I am only surprised the mighty Unluckies do not merely laugh in the face of disapproval.”

Angharad ground her teeth and did not reply. The situation was becoming untenable, that was the truth of it, and she was not so certain that facing down the ketos would truly solve it. They reached the Dregs all too slowly and Angharad did not let herself stop and look around, instead cutting straight to the back of the room. There the others we were waiting: Shalini, who had agreed to be present, and Izel’s oen suggestion.

Yaotl Acatl did not wear the same face paint she once had, now keeping to a simple band of black across the face at the height of her eyes, but otherwise seemed little changed by the year’s debacles. Angharad envied that dauntlessness some, and the princess wore it well – she was still a tall, shapely woman with a sharp beauty. Angharad did not let her gaze linger, however. She and Shalini had never discussed the seriousness of their entanglement, and it was early days yet, but the implication had always been there that a single bed would kept to so long as bed was kept.

She slid into a seat facing the other two, pointedly refraining from pulling Lindiwe a chair, and spared Shalini a smile – which was returned. Her lover had not promised to join the effort, but offered that should the plan suit her she would consider joining.

“Good evening,” she said. “Yaotl, thank you for-”

“Yes,” Yaotl Acatl interrupted.

“Pardon?”

“Yes, I will join your ketos hunt,” the princess patiently said, as if dealing with someone a little slow.

“You don’t want to hear the plan first?” Shalini asked.

“Their captain is not incompetent,” Yaotl shrugged. “And Izel would not countenance a sacrifice play, so the plan should be sound. Who would _not_ want to slay such a mighty creature?”

“Someone uninterested in giving the Unluckies that honor,” Lindiwe said.

Yaotl sneered at her. Lindiwe sneered back. Shalini tried to sneer at them both, but it mostly looked like she was about to sneeze.

“I see no one else offering a berth on a ship headed for that fight,” Yaotl said. “Honor is won blade in hand, it is not for others to give.”

“And how well has that philosophy worked out for you, Izcalli?” Lindiwe smiled.

The princess’ eyes flicked across the table, as if measuring if she could catch the other woman by the hair and smash her into the tabletop in hand, and before that could become a very real possibility Angharad cleared her throat.

“Thank you, Yaotl,” she said. “I am pleased to welcome you to the crew.”

“So what is the plan that Song cooked up, exactly?” Shalini said, after sparing a moment to send Lindiwe a superior look.

Angharad smiled at her.

“I’m sure you’ll find-”

She was interrupted by the sound of chair being dragged. Angharad’s gaze flicked there and she found the one at the end of the table being taken out, only for a languid Musa Shange to drop down into it.

“Ladies, I see you’re coming to terms,” he said. “Good.”

“Musa,” she evenly said. “Can I help you?”

“You can,” Musa Shange said. “Cut me in.”

There was a beat of stillness.

“Pardon?” she asked.

“Cut me in,” Musa repeated. “I want to slay this ketos.”

Angharad’s mind whirled. There were too many possible angles here for her to be sure what this was about. Glory, the Ninth wanting to show up the First? A play against Cao? Or perhaps it was all to keep an eye on the Thirteenth for Morcant, to sabotage them from the inside.

“Given the circumstances, that seems difficult,” she said.

“Let me make it simple, then,” Musa said. “I am calling in my favor.”

Her lips thinned.

“You’re serious?”

“I am.”

“Why?” she asked.

“Are you perhaps unfamiliar with how favors work, Angharad? They are usually lighter on questions.”

She gritted her teeth.

“You know why I balk,” she said.

“I so swear I do not make this request with the intention to harm any effort to kill the ketos,” he replied without batting an eye. “So unless you are to break your word, Angharad, I will be on that most interesting skimmer when it sails out.”

“I am not the only one who must agree,” she said.

“Then remind Song Ren that only weaklings take slights, and we are not that,” Musa coldly said. “It is one thing to refuse overtures, another to treat us as enemies before blade is drawn.”

Lindiwe, amused, cleared her throat.

“Well, it seems we’re to be five,” she said. “How bracing! Now, I do believe you were about to tell us the Ren’s plan.”

Angharad got promises of silence first, of course, since some might still walk. But once she was done explaining, none did and that told her they’d stick through. They were in. Now what they needed was ships enough the fight would not begin and end with the ketos’s jaw closing around the sides of the skimmer.

That was, thankfully, Song’s job to arrange. She had done her part.

--

Colonel Fermin Azocar was looking down at the stage of the Old Playhouse when Song arrived, but not from one of the lower rings.

Instead of the lodges-turned-garden he’d sat down on one of the benches higher up, far from where the nobles had been. The old man was whittling away at a piece of driftwood with a folding knife, scattering wood shavings everywhere. He was also, Song idly noted, wielding the knife with his left hand while he usually held his cane with his right. Was he ambidextrous? She slipped onto the bench, keeping a distance of a few feet as much out of respect as because she did not want any of those wood chips on her.

“Sir.”

“Captain Ren,” the old man said. “Fancy meeting you here.”

“If you truly wanted to pretend this is an accidental encounter, there are less public venues.”

“The irony of doing this in sight of the Galleries appealed,” Azocar said.

He shaved off a piece, flicked it to the ground.

“Also, I don’t care enough to put in the effort.”

Song said nothing, watching him wield the knife with precise nonchalance. The way the edge of the blade faced his thumb went against everything she had been taught about handling naked blades, but it was not her place to say anything. He was evidently an old hand at whittling.

“I read your proposal,” Azocar said. “How sure are you that your tinker’s work will harm the ketos?”

“As sure as we can be without actually using it on the beast,” Song said. “The calculations are solid and it has been used on a lemure to the theorized effect.”

He hummed.

“I’ve had one of my captains check on the Sheba Bastion,” he said. “The chiropters are still there, but nothing else appears to have moved in.”

It had been extremely embarrassing not to know the name of the bat-monsters when writing her report, so Song had been sure to research it afterwards. They were not usually native to this part of the Trebian Sea, someone making excuses would say.

“Glad news,” Song murmured. “Will you be seizing the wharf, then?”

She had recommended as much in her report. Holding the water gate and preventing the ketos from closing it was crucial to any expedition into the depths: otherwise the creature could cut off their retreat at will. It had not bothered to do so last time, but then it had no reason to fear a single ship. It might be more inclined to strand a flotilla and pick it off at its leisure.

“Tomorrow afternoon my galleasses will move in,” Colonel Azocar revealed. “Dedicated gun crews can handle chiropters, if they’ve had forewarning, so we should be able to take it without significant losses.”

He paused, the knife sliding against a solid knot in the wood, and shifted around the piece to take another angle. Song ran the timeline through in her mind: today was sixthday, so presuming slight no losses the ships might be ready for a fight as early as firstday. Gods, finally good news. Tristan looked about to bolt, these days, and Angharad was hardly better.

“The ketos is an issue,” Azocar continued, “but unless everyone who handed in a report was gravely mistake about the dimensions of the water gate it is too large to get through.”

“Its tentacles are not,” Song warned.

“I’d burn candles to the Sleeping God, if it were dumb enough to try that,” he snorted. “The first thing we’ll do after taking that wharf is put cannons on it and point them at the gate. If it peeks its head out, it will get a helping of salt munitions.”

That should secure the gates, Song silently agreed. So long as they put up something in the stairs to prevent lemures wandering down from the bastion above. No creature would have bothered when there was nothing below save the chiropters, but now that there’d be soldiers and smells something was bound to get curious. Still, a man didn’t make colonel in the Watch without knowing how to put up an outpost in hostile territory. She would be doing herself no favors by warning a cautious man.

“With our line of retreat secured an expedition becomes feasible,” Song said. “How many ships are you willing to commit to the hunt?”

The carrack was too large to even enter the cavern, but the four galleasses and the barque under Azocar’s command should all be able to fit. The latter was a glorified supply ship, though, unfit for real combat. She expected only the galleasses, and not all of them either. _Three will be enough_, she thought. Two, though? Two would get tricky.

“None,” Azocar flatly said.

Song blinked.

“Is Lord Asher no longer pressuring you to advance the delve?”

“He’s been to visit me twice, the old crab,” Azocar said, clicking his tongue. “But I’m under the authority of the Obscure Committee as a whole, girl, not any single member of it.”

“I know that,” Song impatiently said. “But Professor He is Cao’s backer and Brigadier Laghari a Stripe. If they have Asher’s vote, they have a majority in the committee and can get rid of you at will.”

“Asher’s not going to give his vote over being blown off,” Azocar told her. “That’s now how Cryptics work when they’re that high up their ladder.”

The knife sliced through wood.

“Call this a free lesson,” the old man said. “The public faces of the Krypteia usually avoid openly taking sides. They _have_ to, otherwise they implicitly give Mask backing to whatever scheme they join – and whatever the outcome of that scheme, afterwards it’s harder for all Masks to do their real job.”

“Cutting out the rot,” Song said.

He nodded.

“No, Asher won’t do anything for the same reason I won’t send ships to back you,” Azocar continued.

She made herself raise an eyebrow, pretending calm as he sliced off a chip.

“My foremost duty is to hold Port Allazei for the Watch, and I barely have the means to do so right now,” Azocar said. “A chunk of the city going up in flames has stirred up lemures again and now anything coming out of the Nettlewood to have a look will find an empty field between it and the savory townsfolk inhabiting the Triangle. Even Templeward is at risk, the gate to it was burned wide open.”

“I’ve not heard of any incursions,” Song slowly said.

“Shuttle-spiders are already setting up in the ashes,” Azocar said. “And last night a hippogriff tried to break into the Galleries through the roof. None have ever ranged that far south before in the years I’ve held this command.”

Song breathed in sharply.

“I’ve petitioned the Obscure Committee for reinforcements, but until they arrive from Lucierna my garrison is stretched thin,” Azocar said. “We have to build and man barricades to protect the entire eastern flank of the Triangle, and now both the College and the Academy are howling in my ear about doubling the guards on their headquarters.”

He spat to the side.

“Like putting up a gunline in front of the Ossurary’s entrance will do a damn thing,” Azocar said. “What we need is screening patrols and a circle of lookouts to stop the Wei girl from torching our houses again, but I don’t have the men or the means for that.”

The knife cut into the wood, getting stuck until he jolted with his wrist.

“Ketos hunts are ship-killers and I cannot afford to lose a ship’s worth of soldiers, Ren,” he said. “I already have too few for my duties.”

She studied him for a moment.

“And taking the wharf should be enough to appease Asher until the men from Lucierna have arrived, in a month or so,” Song said.

Gods, it was a horrid timeline but it was still better than nothing. She had to bring _something _back to her brigade.

“More like two months,” Azocar said. “The increased garrison when they reopened Scholomance already drew from the heart of the Trebian Northwest command, Marshal Camaron will pull soldiers out of the coastal forts to send us this time.”

Which meant sending word to those spread-out forts, ferrying the soldiers to Lucierna and then off to Tolomontera. At least two weeks added, and that was with good winds and no trouble at sea.

“My brigade cannot wait two months,” Song quietly said.

“I know,” Azocar said, chipping at the wood again. “It’s why I decided you were owed the courtesy of a face-to-face.”

A cold comfort, Song thought.

“Is there nothing that can be done?” she asked, almost pleadingly.

“After your rat hit up Cao’s private storage for money I thought there might be something,” Azocar said. “She was stirred up, visited the place that same night. But besides sending a complaint and moving a bag of gems to replace the paper money she hasn’t done anything. I’m guessing the gems are cursed, she has some connections among the Akelarre.”

He shook his head.

“The most I can squeeze out is letting your brigade borrow powder from the force I’ll install on the wharf and let you repay it at cost whenever you have the spare coin,” he said. “You’re not the only one with eyes on you – with Cao’s stock on the rise, she’s moving to take over the defense of the city. If I do you favors, she’ll pounce on it.”

“That _fucking_ fire,” Song snarled. “It has done so much good for her that I can only wonder if...”

“No,” Azocar firmly said. “She’s cutthroat, but not at the expense of the black. Cao hasn’t been snipped by the Krypteia because she uses her leverage to get things done that benefit the order – they just also happen to benefit her career.”

He drummed his fingers.

“Where the Wei girl got that pitch and oil, however, is a concern,” he admitted. “I’ve had a census taken of our supplies and she didn’t hit one of our warehouses to get them. Either Scholomance had a stash that the Machinist told her where to find, or she got her hands on someone’s private things.”

Or, Song thought, someone had handed Cai Wei those supplies. Someone desperate, who needed the Unluckies to be driven out of town and knew Colonel Cao would do everything she could to get it done. Someone with money and ties to ships. Her fingers clenched. It was just a guess, a suspicion, but the more she thought of it...

“Thank you for the courtesy, sir,” she finally said, getting up.

 Azocar studied her for a moment.

“Good luck, Song Ren,” he finally said.

They would need it, she thought, because she suspected that a part of her brigade would be pushing for the expedition to happen even if they had to go at it alone. _And I’m not sure I can refuse without breaking the Thirteenth._

--

Song had offered to come, but Maryam declined. This was better handled by them alone.

The meal was hearty, simple fare – they’d sprung for goat cheese and decent ale, the foremost luxury of it – and the mood was fine even though the adults among the Orels must know why she had come. Word of the garrison’s seizing of the lower rungs of the Sheba Bastion had spread yesterday, but so had Colonel Azocar’s declaration that he had sent for reinforcements and was withholding the garrison from further expeditions until they’d arrived.

Young Koval was sent off after the meal, Maryam’s gaze lingering on his back.

“He seems to be doing well,” Hooks said.

“He’s had nightmares about being taken,” his father tightly replied. “But then so have I. We can only thanks the gods that Izel was there.”

“Best thank the man instead,” Bolic drawled. “He’s a fine hand with a mace.”

Maryam’s lips tightened. The elder Koval had been arranging for the younger to attend the local Watch school, but now the plans were set aside. It would be months before either felt safe enough to be far from the other. She couldn’t blame them: if Morcant hadn’t decided that getting the Unluckies expelled would be more practical than using a hostage, the boy would be in the slaver’s hands right now.

They let the conversation ebb low, after, and when Old Horvat was done clearing the plates they turned to the reason for her visit.

“We intend to go forward with the expedition even without the garrison’s support,” Maryam told them.

And, potentially, without most the Skiritai that Angharad had gathered on their behalf. They’d signed onto a plan that counted on that support.

“We have done everything we can to stack the odds our way,” Hooks said, “but the risks will not be small.”

Maryam cleared her throat.

“The first minute of the fight tells us if we make it,” she said. “Hooks and I will be keeping watch, but if the ketos lunges out from below the ship without us catching it in time there is little we can do. If it surfaces and _then _attacks, however, we believe in a victory.”

“How likely is it to attack from below?” Koval the Elder bluntly asked.

“It’s difficult to say,” Maryam admitted. “Usually a ketos would not try to eat a ship made of metal, but this one has been stuck below for who knows how long. After we gave it the slip last time it might not want to chance another escape.”

“I’ll go,” Bolic spoke into the silence.

Eyes flicked his way.

“Regardless of duties owed to the princess of the Izvoric, we signed on to serve aboard a blackclad ship,” Bolic said. “It might not be a warship, but neither is it a pleasure barge. Danger is part of the bargain.”

“Well said,” Old Horvat coughed into his hand. “To desist now would be going back on oaths.”

“We’re giving you the out on purpose,” Hooks said. “Oaths or not. No one should be on that ship that doesn’t want to be.”

“I _don’t _want to be,” Poltava frankly said. “But Bolic’s right that this is what we signed up for. And it won’t be the last time either, will it?”

“We don’t intend to go looking for sea monsters,” Maryam hedged, “but going back and forth across the Trebian Sea it’s inevitable we’ll run into some.”

“This isn’t some chance encounter, Poltava, it’s going to that lake for a death match with a shiptaker,” Koval the Elder sharply said. “These are not the same thing.”

“Oh, just refuse and be done with it,” Bolic scorned. “We all know you will.”

“That’s enough,” Hooks sharply said.

“This isn’t a court game, it is a genuine offer to pass on the fight,” Maryam added. “So there’ll be no more of that – we wouldn’t be making the offer if we didn’t endorse any of you taking it.”

That actually had Poltava hesitating, but in the end only the elder Koval desisted. He tried to explain, but they waved him off.

“It doesn’t need explaining,” Hooks said. “You have a son.”

It was one thing to head into the dark knowing there were creatures in it, another to set sail intending to _fight _them. Maryam had intended to stay a little longer, to ask about Young Koval’s personal schooling and Horvat’s continued investigation of local brews – he was on a quest to find a ‘proper coastlands beer’, much disdaining the local fare – but the sound of a crowd gathering outside put an end to that. Hooks popped her head to the wall to check it wasn’t a mob out for Unluckies blood.

That’d be a sharp escalation, but those happened more than she would like these days.

“They’re gathering near port,” she said.

So Maryam put on her cloak and pulled down her hood before taking to the street, Hooks matching her. Using a shaping the same cloak, as if Tristan had stolen _her_ one as well.

“He would if I asked,” Hooks insisted.

“But he didn’t,” Maryam happily replied.

They did not bicker all the way to the gatehouse, because when Maryam informed her sister of the correct order of things it was not an argument but a lesson. One delivered to an ungrateful, quarrelsome brat. Pushing through the last of the crowd and striding through the pillared shadows, they emerged into the Orrery light to finally get a look at what had everyone gathering.

Ships.

Ten – no, eleven of them. Three tall galleons formed the heart of the formation sailing for Port Allazei, flanked by two pairs of fighting carracks bristling with guns. Prowling around them like sleek, oared wolves were the five galleasses rounding out the numbers. All flew the black, but there was chatter around from someone who’d brought a longview and had more to say. Instead of going begging Maryam and Hooks traced Gloam, forming a slightly wobbly Eyecatcher – they were falling behind on Autarchics - in front of their right eye.

The square of Gloam was burned with everything the eye saw but could not discern, the sisters then closing in on the detail of the flag. It was a bronze diagonal cross with the letter W in the same shade filling the left space, all on Watch black. The killed the Eyecatcher a heartbeat later.

“Western Fleet,” Maryam breathed out. “They’re here early.”

It seemed like she was going to need Song after all.

--Getting aboard the _Bad News_, the towering and heavily-armed galleon that was Admiral Zokufa’s flagship, proved much easier than Maryam had anticipated.

Her and Song being essentially summoned to attend to the admiral within an hour of docking really cut down on the time making inquiries about when the man might be available. Hooks had not been sent for, so she rode Maryam’s body instead as they were guided to the raised aft deck with its large, luxurious cabin. Black-clad sailors ushered them in, closing the door behind them with a soft click. Standing behind a polished wooden deck was the man himself, already watching them.

Admiral Zokufa was younger than Maryam had thought a man whose sobriquet was ‘Old Stormy’ would be.

He was not young, mind you, but couldn’t be much older than fifty. The groomed, puffy beard that framed his face was threaded black and white, but the dark skin made leathery by a life at sea was not yet measurably creased. His fleshy nose was almost triangular, cornered by deep laugh lines on a stern face and large, thick and heavily-rimmed glasses ate up much of the face under a receding hairline. Zokufa had pale brown eyes that looked oddly gentle, given his sharp military bearing.

“Sit,” the admiral invited them, pointing at the padded chairs before his desk. “Brandy?”

They both demurred, which had the man looking pleased. He did not pour himself a glass either. His gaze moved to Song.

“Fermin tells me that you are unusually reasonable for a Stripe,” Admiral Zokufa said. “I’ll grant you the benefit of the doubt. Tell me everything about the ketos.”

Song admirably summed up three different reports and the Thirteenth’s own preparations without being imprecise or running long, which was a sort of magic Maryam could only admire. Zokufa slowly nodded. He remained silent for a moment, thoughtful, then his gaze moved on.

“Khaimov,” he said. “Captain Tianming speaks well of you.”

She coughed into her fist.

“And I think well of him,” Maryam said.

“The man is a rogue and romantic,” Zokufa mildly said. “He has read too many Ramayan serials.”

The admiral drummed his fingers against his desk.

“But he is not a fool,” he conceded. “What are your expectations, for the deal you offer?”

“Expectations?”

“It is a pleasing bargain,” Admiral Zokufa said. “We seize ships and squeeze slavers. But I will not have a student brigade swan around the Trebian Sea claiming that the Western Fleet owes them. What do you want?”

“What the terms set out,” Maryam honestly said. “I don’t expect anything more.”

Pale brown eyes moved to Song, a graying eyebrow risen above the glasses.

“She means it,” Song said. “And we have no intention of swaggering as if we were your very own princelings, sir.”

She paused.

“To be frank, the idea that you would do us a fair turn is out of step with our experiences with officers of your rank.”

His lips thinned.

“I would chide you for that,” Zokufa said, “but I have seen it turn worse in my lifetime. The Conclave’s leadership bankruptcy has let the weeds grow in. The order is the largest and most powerful it has been, but also the most gangrenous.”

He shook his head.

“There is no point in making apologies for what is,” Admiral Zokufa said. “The only fitting answer to rot is the torch.”

He stepped away from the desk, taking a dipping pen and ink from a stand, then returned to pull out a sheet from his desk that he signed without even a hint of flourish before handing it to Maryam.

“The legal arrangement you proposed is accepted,” he said.

Matter of fact, like he was passing her a fork instead of bringing Izvoric into the fleet. Like he’d not just agreed to using prize ships and traps to free more of her people and cloak them in black. Maryam sagged into her seat, unspeakably relieved. She’d hoped, had let herself hope, but… But it was done now, signed ink on paper. That stroke of a pen had done more to help the Izvoric  on this side of the sea than she’d thought she might manage in her lifetime. Song squeezed her arm and she faintly smiled back.

She would haver thanked Zokufa, if he did not seem like the kind of man who would be insulted by it.

“I will require your help in a separate matter, Captain Ren,” the admiral continued, eyes returned to Song.

They clenched up. A last-minute price?

“Sir?”

“My flotilla will be resting in Allazei for a month before we begin operations in the region,” Admiral Zokufa said, “but practice is necessary to maintain one’s edge. Are you aware of any nearby body water where galleasses might practice monster-hunting maneuvers?”

Maryam choked. Was he really…

“We could guide you to one,” Song croaked. “Tough there has been a report of a ketos there.”

“A shame it will not reach my desk in time,” Zokufa said, in the tone of someone who would ensure so.

He dismissed them, after, and Maryam should have taken the hint. She didn’t.

“Why?” she asked, on her feet. “Why help us? No one else your rank has ever done anything like this.”

Zokufa considered her through his glasses.

“The order has never been perfect,” he said, tone impassive. “But when I first enrolled you would not have thought to ask that question, because the answer ought to be obvious.”

His jaw clenched.

“Duty is not transaction,” he said. “An oath is not a bargain. I am an admiral of the Watch, and when the Old Night dares to present itself to my guns I shall fire them until it crawls back into the pit.”

The older man sat back down in his seat, something all too weary flashing behind those glasses before the iron fell back into place.

“Because I am sorry you had to ask,” Admiral Zokufa said, and nothing more.

 

# Chapter 61

The Orrery light was golden and distant, like a king’s disdain cast upon the world.

Izel spared it little attention, consumed as he was with the last checks on the greater lenslight – work made ever more urgent by the Sheba Bastion’s rapidly approaching contour. Maryam was making more than good time, having grown comfortable enough with the route to shave off minutes. A look revealed that the belly screws were all tightened properly so Izel pushed off from the metal bones of the turret, wiping his hands on his coat.

He’d already checked the aether-forged lenses for hairline cracks, but he made sure to test the handholds one last time: the brass grips were cool to the touch and moved smoothly, letting him orient the box of the lenslight. The core of the machine had not significantly changed, having mostly been remade larger and with accommodations for larger gas canisters. The major departures from the old frame were in the segmented tripod and the twin handholds on the back of the box, changing the lenslight from a fixed lance to something that could be aimed.

That made it twice he’d run the checks now, but his hands were already itching for a third. A cleared throat startled him out of the thought, Angharad standing by his side in her killing-finery: the black coat of the Watch and steel clasped at her side, pistol and rifle secured.

“Captain Ren sends an order to take a breath and to cease worrying yourself into an early grave,” Angharad drily said.

He grimaced.

“I’ll stop,” he conceded, shoving the cloth in a pocket. “I think it’s nerves about the ship.”

And where it was headed, and who else was on it. Yaotl was giving him a wide berth, staying near the prow with the harpoon that had her swaggering for some reason, but she had come. That was something, and a something he was not yet ready to unravel. He’d just been getting used to the idea of that bridge being ash, the thought that it might not be was difficult in a different way.

“I am told that Izcalli are not a sailing people,” Angharad said.

Izel chuckled.

“That’s something of an understatement.”

The kingdom owned two large and well-armed fleets, but it did not have a strong naval tradition and what successes it’d had at sea mostly preceded the rise of Malan as a great power. There’d been an ironic span during the Century of Crowns where Izcalli had been the preeminent naval power of Aurager, but that’d largely been because every other rival was busy with unification, collapse or being invaded.

Arguably, the Kingdom of Izcalli existed at all because of its weakness at sea. The Succession Wars had begun when King Chongsheng of Cathay saw that the wealthy southern coast was ripe for the taking and promptly invaded. His success had in turn allowed the House of Toxtle to unite the Seven Valleys and begin the work of unifying all of Izcalli under one banner without southern rivals constantly sabotaging them.

Even in modern days, the finest sailors among Aztlan peoples were from Tariac and Totochtin. The kingdom heavily recruited from the cities of the latter for naval officers, which Father had once told him was half the reason why the kingdom needed to keep recruiting from Totochtin for naval officers. The other half was that sailing was usually seen as belonging to the Trade Sphere. Not warrior’s work.

“There is not a single warrior society dedicated to naval warfare,” Izel told her.

“Really?” Angharad said, brow raising. “Not a single one? I thought the societies of the War Sphere to be quite comprehensive.”

“There have been attempts to secure such rites, over the centuries, but they were stamped out by the Calendar Court,” Izel said. “The royal house owns no coastland, so they fear such a society would naturally lean the way of the Sunflower Lords.”

And the warrior societies were a crucial part of how the Grasshopper Kings maintained control over their every-unruly vassals. A king who allowed them to bend the way of the Sunflower Lords would not be king for long.

“Both Malan and Peredur boast of raising the finest sailors in the world,” Angharad told him, then cleared her throat. “I am partial to the Pereduri claim, of course.”

“Of course,” Izel smiled.

“But I will concede that Malani explorers have some great discoveries to their name.”

Indeed, Malani seafarers had all but named the Century of Sails: during the preceding Dominion they had found the Wrecking Isles, Glare-touched islands on the far side of the Aetolian Ocean, and from there discovered the ancient wonder known as the Western Canals – beyond which lay the enormous sprawl of the westerlands, the western continent on which Malan was settling colonies.

“You mother was an explorer of some repute, I hear,” Izel hazarded.

Captain Rhiannon Tredegar - Sizani Maraire, as her name in the official records went – had famously discovered a passage through the Western Canals, freeing Malani ships from the need to sail around them and chance the hazardous northern passage called the Ranging Way.

“She was,” Angharad replied, tone melancholy. “She loved the sea, my mother. Staying on land for too long had her on pins and needles.”

She cleared her throat.

“But I did not much take to sailing myself, so I will confess that ships are no great love of mine,” she said. “I can offer some sympathy as to the nature of your nerves – I would rather this journey be over with.”

He side-eyed her and found, to his unsurprised disbelief, that she seemed entirely serious. As if the plan she found more enticing than the trip into the dark was not magnitudes more dangerous. Izel was effectively deputized as an artilleryman for the day, a position not without peril, but at least he was not planning to board the ketos like it was some island instead of a massive, furious monster trying to kill them all.

“Skiritai,” he sighed, shaking his head to an unwarrantedly baffled look from her.

He went to check on the lantern in the back, where Song would not be in position to see him fuss. While the design had originally been meant for the turret now occupied by the lenslight, and thus taken some time to reposition at the aft of the ship, he’d built the structure with an eye to flexibility from the start. It wouldn’t be quite as well-secured as when it had been anchored in the turret, but unless a powerful force tried to wrench it forward the device should be in no danger of coming loose.

He would have soldered the base of the device to the floor, but Maryam had threatened to solder him to his own buttocks and spoken the threat with such utter seriousness he’d not been able to laugh it off. She was quite protective over the looks of the skimmer.

From the back he could see the galleasses following behind them, three-masted ships with black triangular sails and protruding oars. The Western Fleet had leant them three ships for the hunt, under the paper-thin pretense of sending them out on exercise, and he’d been assured that all three officers were Trebian Sea veterans with experience fighting men and monsters at sea. _Not that we would have been able to turn them away even if they were green as grass._

They could not keep up with the skimmer, not even with the wind at their back, but then it was only to be expected from warships armed to the teeth and thus much heavier than the skimmer. All three galleasses bore forty cannons of different sizes, a handful on the forecastle and the aft but with the vast majority on the sides of the ship. Broadsides would be the source of monster-killing volleys, not head-on chases.

“Quite a sight, aren’t they?”

This time he’d not been so lost in thought to miss the approach, though the sound of the waves had mostly covered for it. He spared Musa Shange the kind of smile you put on for Candle priests and court grandees, friendly and fixed solidly in place no matter what was about to be said.

“Not so impressive as the galleons, but then I hear the Western Fleet has few of those,” Izel said.

“Only five, Sebastian says,” Musa replied. “Admiral Zokufa brought more than half his heaviest warships to visit Tolomontera.”

A pause.

“One might call that heavy-handed, were they so inclined.”

“Are you?” Izel said.

“Not at the moment,” Musa carelessly shrugged. “I find it interesting that the Thirteenth has ties to the admiralty, but I come for a different reason.”

“To this ship or to this conversation?”

“Yes,” Musa laughed. “But I shall not tease overmuch, Master Coyac. My captain again extends inquiries over sale of the blastcap design.”

And finally Izel had a marginally less frustrating answer to give him.

“It will become available on the ketos has been dealt with,” he said.

Song had conceded that he needed the money badly enough that trying to hold back the design for favors was no longer worth it. Thank the gods for that, broke was almost too kind a word for the state of his funds.

“Glad news, glad news,” Musa said, hands resting on the railing.

His tone was entirely casual, which had Izel’s hackles rising. He wasn’t acting like someone who’d just gotten the answer they had come for.

“And this new device, the one mounted in front of the ship?”

And there it was.

“Unrelated,” Izel evenly said. “And still a work in progress. It will be a long time until I am ready to sell it.”

Never was quite a long time, after all. Musa shrugged.

“As you say,” he replied. “I am curious to see what it will do, that the likes of Song Ren and Angharad are willing to bet our lives on its effectiveness.”

The prick to his pride twinged and a defense was halfway to his lips before he swallowed it. Musa Shange would already see more than Izel would like, he would not let anger grant the man anything more than what his eyes might gather.

“As you say,” Izel replied with studied pleasantness.

Musa eyed him, smiled, and with a pat on the shoulder swaggered away to join the rest of the Skiritai on the deck. Izel watched him leave with thinned lips as the skimmer began lining up with the mouth of the Sheba Bastion. He didn’t know why Musa Shange was here, but he’d put blade to finger it wasn’t for the hunt.

The man was after something, and Izel could only hope that his suspicion as to what came from arrogance.

--

Plans had been made to convene one final time with the Western Fleet officers before the ships went through the gate, so Song asked Maryam to dock near the end of the waterway.

There was no sign left of the chiropters, not even corpses, but her silver eyes saw holes and scorch marks in the ceiling where muskets had been fired. The occupation of the Sheba Bastion’s bottom level was an orderly thing: Colonel Azocar’s men had fortified their corner of the wharf, barricading the stairs with filled-up crates and setting up two batteries with cannons stripped from their ship.

One, carrying all the heavy guns, was pointed at the darkness beyond the gate. The other had prudently been arrayed to face the mouth of the cavern, in case a sea creature happened to get curious. The captain in charge had been informed with last night’s shift change that the flotilla would be coming, so the man quite decently welcomed Song with a warm liquid that could claim to be tea-adjacent and a tin of biscuits.

The courtesy was also extended to the two fleet officers that came ashore, Commodore Acahua and Captain Beristain. The former shook Song’s hand, the short and heavily tattooed Izcalli complimenting Maryam’s navigation of the local waters. He gulped down his cup in a single swallow, ignoring how it was scalding hot, while the Lierganen captain accompanying him tore her way through the biscuits with relentless eagerness.

The commodore had already been part of a ketos hunt, Song had been informed, though only as a sailor and not from a ship that’d come close to the beast. Still, he had monster-hunting experience in spades. Captain Beristain, on the other hand, was here in large part because she was the second-in-command of the triad of ships and would be taking command should Acahua perish.

“It’s a brave thing you’re doing, going in as bait,” the commodore said. “But I will be blunt, Warrant Officer Ren: if you get sunk, I’ll not risk my ships to fish out your people unless the ketos was put to flight.”

“Nor would I expect you to,” Song assured him. “As discussed, it is our role make the beast surface and keep it in place for you. Your role is to bring to bear the firepower we do not have.”

The man nodded in something that was not quite approval, but not too far off.

“Then I wish you luck,” Commodore Acahua said, offering his hand to shake.

She was startled by how genuinely friendly the gesture was, but smoothed it off her face as she shook the hand. A disgruntled noise from Beristain had Song turning a wary look her way, Commodore Acahua raising an eyebrow at the dark-haired woman.

“Is it true your skimmer doesn’t have a name, Ren?” Captain Beristain asked.

Song blinked, then slowly nodded.

“You should take care of that,” the captain said. “It’s bad luck to leave a ship nameless.”

Beristain traced a circle on the back of her hand, to the commodore’s open eye-rolling.

“Gods save me from Circle-botherers.”

“They won’t,” Beristain muttered under her breath. “All the good gods are on the Orthodoxy’s side.”

It sounded like a long-running argument and Song had no intention of sticking her oar in bickering that didn’t sound particularly fond, so instead she gave a platitude about considering it and retreated back to her ship. She did not know what reason the Khaimov sisters had for not naming the ship, but she had no intention of pressing them regarding the matter on behalf of some stranger’s superstitions.

She did head towards the sisters, however, to give the order to set out. Hooks and Maryam hid it well, but she could tell their nerves were strung out at the thought of what was to come.

“I do not expect miracles of you,” Song gently said. “We have done all we can to stack the odds our way.”

“I know,” Maryam tightly said.

“But you’re not the one watching for jaws coming from below that would kill everyone here,” Hooks grunted out, leaning against the glass wall. “If you could, we’d have you strapped down there and looking.”

“The drowning might be something of a hindrance to giving alarm,” Song said, letting herself be drawn in.

A few thrown hatchets always made them feel better.

“Sound like shirker talk,” Maryam said with a put-on sneer. “A real Stripe would just think of the order and hold her breath.”

“Thus I am revealed an impostor,” Song drily said, clapping her friend’s shoulder and smiling at Hooks. “You two should come join us when you pass the wheel to Bolic.”

“Standing in the middle of a band of Skiritai murder-stroking their blades like they’re firstborns?” Maryam skeptically said. “You have the strangest ideas of a good time, Song.”

“She also gets weird about her rifle,” Hooks noted. “This might be a birds of a feather situation.”

“I have not yet decided who will tally our powder expenditure after the expedition,” Song warned.

They both hastily withdrew any implication that Song might clean her rifle more than was strictly necessary by the unfit maintenance standards of others, and went away satisfied in the knowledge that order had been restored. It was only natural that she should head towards the prow of the ship, on the way trading nods with the Skiritai gathered around Angharad. What they were up to might ungenerously be described by some as murder-stroking weapons.

She left the mirror-dancer to it: unlike her, Angharad had the respect of the band and the natural authority to lead them. It had been a simple matter to informally deputize her as a lieutenant over the others and have orders handed down through her, sparing Song the risk of the kind of denial that would damage the fiction of her authority. After all, for all that she was mostly the one giving out orders she did not actually outrank anyone on this ship.

Her place near the prow was not empty, Tristan already standing there as somewhere behind them Maryam eased the skimmer off the stone wharf. Even further behind the galleasses of the Western Fleet were doing the same, though their sails were pulled up and it was oars that were pushing them off the wharf. Tristan looked tired, as he always did these days, but there was a grimly determined cast to him as the ship was aimed at the second water gate.

The constant delays in reaching Fortuna were eating away at him, but he’d been able to choke it down because they were in sight of an ending. If they had not been, Song suspected that his thinning patience would already be ripped right through. There was no chance of that ending up anything but an ugly business.

“Ready?” he asked before she could.

A rote answer was on the tip of her tongue, but a gray-eyed look stopped it there. She sighed, leaning her elbows against the railing. After a moment she glanced down at her palms, closing them into fists. She could not see anything below the skin, could not feel it, but Captain Yue had shown her it was there nonetheless. How odd that she could come to plan on it, count on it.

“I do not think I can be ready for such a thing,” Song admitted. “But I am as prepared as I can be, that will have to suffice.”

“We’re all riding closer to the edge, these days,” Tristan said.

She hummed in agreement.

“Ready?” she echoed.

“My role is simple enough,” he shrugged. “I’m little more than a signalman for this one.”

“Which bothers you, when today’s skirmish is the gate to Fortuna,” she guessed.

He eyed her for a moment, then looked away.

“I would feel more at ease were it in my hands,” he conceded. “Instead of seemingly everybody else’s.”

“We can sail out today only because of the funds you provided,” Song reminded him.

He snorted.

“I have not been afflicted with a taste for the heroic, Song, don’t worry,” Tristan said. “I don’t envy your role to play. I’m just... unused to asking others to carry the bag for me.”

“I can sympathize,” she murmured.

“I expect you can,” he said just as quietly.

They crossed the invisible line of the water gate, the cool of the dark washing over them like a cold breath, and Tristan shivered.

“Best I get to my perch,” he said. “Draw first, Song.”

“Red days and jade nights,” she wished back.

He went away, light-footed as a cat, and she was left alone to look into the abyss.

It was hard to tell when they crossed into the grasp of Scholomance. The water gate must lead _somewhere_ that wasn’t the smoky, haunted waterways beneath the ground, but at some point over the years Scholomance’s grasp has crept far enough it was able to seize upon the water and make it lead into itself. It might have been as small an opening as a hall beneath Scholomance coming too close to one of the waterways, allowing the god to claw through the wall to reach it.

Once they reached the still obsidian surface of the lake, though, there was no mistaking where they were.

It should not have been possible for so vast a cavern to smell musty, but somehow it did. Cold, wet and musty without so much as a hint of salt – what water lay here either had not come from the sea or come to be estranged from it. Were it simple darkness here, Song’s eyed would see through it. It was not. Izel’s lantern, the bubble of light through which they sailed, thinned the dark even beyond its immediate cast but beyond that thinned layer lay Gloam as Song had hardly seen it before.

The thick, oily darkness moved like solid winds – a living painting in dark, blowing and coiling around itself. Song sometimes caught glimpses through the gaps, but it was like looking at a veil of living smoke. This must be what the Gloam was like out on the Straying Sea, where it grew so dense that Gloam storms blew every day, slamming against this coast and that.

There would be signs, though. The Gloam moved in currents, but most of these were unhurried and almost lazy. When the ketos had come last time, Song had seen the storm taking shape even as the monster stirred it into being. Her eyes moved from one curl to another, looking for any hint, but there were none. Not so far behind them the three galleasses were following, long oars dipping into the water as they chased the tireless advance of the skimmer.

Song was on edge, but the currents of Gloam remained unstirred as they sailed into the dark. Had the ketos yet to see them, or was it drawing them further away from the gate?

It was difficult to remain at full attention for a long span of time, but fingernails biting into her palm and chewing at the inside of her cheek kept her readiness from waning too much. It was waiting for them to falter, to stop paying attention. Maryam had some time ago left the captain’s cabin behind and moved onto the deck, where she sat cross-foot near the turret with her sister nowhere in sight – gone below, no doubt, to see if the creature was lurking. The Skiritai were keeping an eye on her from a distance.

The wheel was in Bolic’s hands, and the pirate might not be trustworthy but he was a fine enough steersman. Song’s teeth and cheeks were aching by the time the darkness parted to reveal a giant silhouette in the distance: the god-mold, the two split half-spheres jutting out of the water. One half had mostly fallen below the waterline, but there was enough still above for the ancient mold to look like some manner of ancient monument.

It was, in a manner of speaking. Only the Antediluvians had built wonders such as this.

Bolic adjusted the course of the skimmer, curving towards the tall structure, but Song’s eyes were not caught on the outer parts. They remained peeled on the insides of the sphere, the ichor-like darkness gathered in the curve like blood in a wound. That was not... natural. They had not come close enough for her to see it, last time, but to her eyes the liquid looked almost alive. Writhing ever so slightly.

She remained spellbound as the skimmer approached the mold, slowing a hair as they came close enough the lantern’s light almost caressed the edge of the stone structure. Song pushed off the railing, tugging down her coat. A glance told her that the galleasses were beginning to trail behind, men pulling oars struggling to keep pace with the finest work out of Asphodel’s shipyards, and it would be dangerous to get too far ahead.

Bolic must be told to curve around, and a decision made as to where they were all headed next. Song moved past the Skiritai, but two strides past was stilled by the sound of someone breathing in sharply.

“Something is here,” Maryam called out, shoulders tensing even as she remained sitting. “Below and behind.”

 Behind? _Shit_. There was only one reason for the ketos to line up like this.

“Bolic,” Song shouted. “Ahead at all speed!”

She dimly registered Angharad exhorting the Skiritai to ready for the fight, and above she could see that Tristan had just shot a red flare without needing to be told. The skimmer thrummed and began to carve deeper into the water, wind picking up around them as one of the galleasses fired back a green flare. Good, Song thought, heart in her throat. She moved towards the back of the ship, rifle at the ready, and was joined by Orel Poltava. The blacksmith had a ‘borrowed’ musket in hand, and though the barrel trembled it was pointed the right way.

“Steady,” Song said.

Even as the wake of the skimmer grew broader and larger, she caught sight of the ripple in the water. Slight but growing by the instant and – and she screamed the same time Maryam did, about the same thing.

“_Lunge!_”

Bolic had been drilled about this very eventuality and did not fail them. He banked hard to the left as the ketos lunged out of the water with snapping jaws, a leviathan-in-the-box, and Song shot at the moving mass more out of hatred than need. Her bullet tore into hide as the ketos massive form slipped past them, close enough a tentacle slapped against the top of the cabin and smashed glass.

Tall waves rippled out as it smashed back into the water, Song desperately grasping at the railing as the ship near toppled over. They were turning to face the ketos but it was turning to face_ them_, and the fucking waves were slowing them down. It’d be ready first, ready to lunge again, but Bolic knew his business: he steered the ship further left, curving around the mold. The ketos disdained sinking back under the waves, instead turning around the mold from the other way, and as the prow of the skimmer went past the edge they came face to face with the monster.

The great, calamitous beast with its open gullet and writhing forest of tentacles, too many of which ended in softly crooning lures. Gods, it was so large – its head alone large as the ship – and the song was urging them all to sleep, to rest, to-

There was a faint flick, the sound of well-oiled metal turning and then of a lever coming down.

“Firing,” Izel Coyac announced, voice perfectly even, and the world went white.

--

The first heartbeat was blinding, like a star shot out of a bottle, but the aftermath was unsettlingly gentle.

Angharad blinked out the ache and found that the mounted lenslight was now no different than a lantern, a simple beam of pale light being shined onto the ketos as Izel aimed the device with brass grips. Only where the light touched the monster’s hide it bubbled up and popped with a sizzling sound, like water on a hot pan. The beam slid across one of the eyes, light as a feather, and the entire thing _burst_ like too full waterskin. Wet, transparent chunks went flying and the ketos let out a noise like a shrieking whale song, echoed by every lure’s mouth.

Bracing!

Musa, standing besides her, was looking at the lenslight with something like awe – and, strangely, regret.

“What a weaponsmith your brigade has found,” he said, shaking his head.

Regret at the relations between their brigades being at such a low ebb, perhaps. Angharad did not have the heart to tell him even fine friendship would have made no difference.

In its throes of pain, the ketos smashed against the side of the grand mold and let out another shriek as the structure trembled. No matter: it had now been long enough for Yaotl Acatl to run up to the prow and with a battle cry make the throw she’d been charged with. The princess’s arm whipped forward and the harpoon flew like an arrow, rope slithering behind, and Angharad allowed herself to admire the arc for a moment.

Yaotl had squarely beaten out Musa when their band tested harpoon-throwing, being familiar with javelins – while Musa’s own experience with hunting spears in turn squarely beat out everyone else in their warband.

The harpoon’s barbed head sunk a little past the nostrils of the boar-like head, biting deeply, but it was so tormented by the lenslight it didn’t even notice. It soon would, though, for Yaotl immediately pulled at the rope. The notion that the skimmer might be able to forcefully keep the beast out of the water if it wanted to dive was absurd, as Professor Kang had made plain to them. This was no whale, and their ship was much too small besides.

No, when Yaotl Acatl pulled at the rope what it did was rip open a handful of skins set around the shaft of the harpoon and splatter a heavy helping of _plousperi_ all over the creature’s nose.

There was a beat of silence as the creature stilled, and then it _heaved_.

“Ready for boarding,” Angharad shouted even as the ketos began to sneeze.

It was no comical sight, not on a monster this size. Every spasm sent tall waves roiling and if it’d hit the ship it might well have dented the hull. Instead Orel Bolic managed to guide the skimmer close to the sneezing beast even as the hunting crew thrummed around her, tense as a pulled string. They settled into a broad triangle with herself and Lindiwe at the front, leaving room within for the two bodies they would be escorting onto the keto’s back: Song and Maryam.

The two had the blank faces of someone thinking too hard about what it meant to board a furious sea monster, so Angharad clapped their shoulders and smiled.

“Think of the story!”

Oddly, this did not reassure. Ah well. They rushed to the prow, Yaotl falling in to turn the triangle into a diamond, and moved to secure their climb onto the trashing beast. It was easier than the dantesvara, at least at first – the beast was larger and it was harder to shake them off from the water, so the climbing spears did their job. Angharad went first, pushing down a somewhat inappropriate whoop when the creature’s thrashing about had her weightless for a moment, and pressed down against the top of the sneezing ketos’ head as a tentacle struck blindly past her.

They climbed, one after another. Maryam almost fell off but Shalini caught her wrist in time, almost pulling that thin arm out of its socket by tugging her back in place. By then Angharad had largely secured her foothold, not that it would help much.

This was not to be a fight, for what lay ahead was not an opponent. Hundreds of writhing tentacles going down the ketos’ back were swinging and grabbing blindly, each whistling as they tore through the air. Each was long length of muscle-flesh, powerful as a kicking horse and entirely capable of snatching a bird out of the air, and their only advantage was that the ketos could not yet see them.

But the _ploupseri _would not keep it above the water much longer, so into peril they must press.

It was not a fight they waded into but a forest. Blades out on the screaming, trashing monster they put the Acallar’s harsh lessons to work: Musa and Shalini on the flanks pinned the tentacles with long spears, while Angharad and Lindiwe waded in to carve at them like they were tree trunks. Her blade, Sleeping God, always seemed to perfectly cut into whatever it touched for the first instant. Lindiwe’s was just as sharp, and if not for those edges all of them would be dead.

Mere steel would not have been enough to cut down those tentacles before they could rip out the spears.

Yet even with those priceless blades and five unflinching Skiritai it was brutal work. To advance was to retreat, ducking out of the way when the ketos’ limbs tried to smash them. Shalini was clipped three steps in, through bad luck dodging one into another, and her shoulder cracked like it was stepped-on kindling.

She let out a hoarse cry but they pushed on, because if they didn’t they would drown. If the ketos went back in the water, it would drag them down with it. They cut and ducked and when lures – men and women, children and elderly – came down to snatch them Musa emptied a pistol in the face of the one who had grabbed Song, cracking open the puppet of bone, while she and Yaotl tore through another with twin swings.

The air kept rippling with whispers and screams and a wailing dirge pounding at their ears, the entire journey hardly a minute long but feeling like an hour, until Maryam called them to a stop at the bottom of a lure-tentacle made headless by Shalini.

“Here,” Maryam shouted. “Song, at the foot.”

“Make a ring,” Angharad made heard over the din. “Cover the two of them.”

The tentacles whipped at them still but they held fast, spears pinning down the appendages long enough for blades to hack at them, and it was all going well until Song knelt by the root of the lure, laying a hand on the flesh, and Maryam in turn put a hand on their captain’s shoulder –

And every single tentacle on the back suddenly shivered before going still.

 --

There was a god on the other side of Song Ren’s soul and Maryam could feel its dreadful hate pouring out into the world.

She could not tell how powerful the nascent curse-god truly was, but she and Hooks got the barest impression of its scope and it felt… gargantuan. A nation’s worth of hatred and spite poured into the aether year after year, eager to reach out and crush the name it had been born to end. Gods, it was like playing with fire to even touch such a thing but they must.

None of them believed they’d survive going into the ketos’ mouth the way the Skiritai of yore had. Those bold madmen usually hadn’t, more often than not.

Maryam reached out for the thing at the heart of Song that was the conduit, the root of the god’s presence, and felt something reach out at her nav through it. But Hooks was wary and quick, and before she could be ripped out and devoured she wove a single string of Gloam between the god and the ketos. Not even a little finger’s width, an anemic little thing.

The curse god poured through it like an ocean crammed down straw, slamming into the ketos, and Maryam let out a wild laugh as she drew away.

“Gods,” Song rasped out. “I can _feel _it.”

So could Maryam, by virtue of still having a hand on Song’s soul. The distant curse-god was using her friend as a bridge to try and seize the ketos, to drown out its mind and turn it into a thrall, but the creature was centuries old and powerful in the way that great and ancient lemures often were. It fought back, wrestled for control of its own body, and the result was exactly what Maryam had theorized.

The ketos stopped moving, going still as a corpse as it floated in the water.

“Ancestors,” Musa said, voice colored with disbelief. “It actually worked.”

It had, Maryam thought. Now there was, however, the slight problem known as the second part of the plan: the galleasses, having mostly caught up and spread out past the mold, turned to offer the ketos the side of their ships. A flare went up, bright red, and in a rolling thunder one of them emptied a broadside into the monster.

The cannonballs ripped into the flesh and smashed bone even as the monster stayed entirely still, mind trashing at the danger but unable to spare even a thought away from the struggle with the god lest it be swallowed whole. This part, immobilizing the ketos so the galleasses could kill it, was working very well. The problem was that it would _stop _working the moment Song took her hand off the lure, and that meant they had to stay on the fucking monster being shot at by the better part of sixty cannons.

A second volley hit the monster, spraying ichor and bone.

One would think this was patently dangerous enough for anyone with sense, but joining the Thirteenth evidently jostled something loose inside skulls so Maryam breathed out and prepared to make this much, much worse. She traced a sense of _now_ against the veil and her sister slipped out of her, fully adorned as a princess of the Izvoric in lace and silver, and ignored the startled Skiritai to raise a hand to firmament.

“Hear me,” Hooks shouted in Recnigvor.

The currents rippled a little around them, Gloam and water both, but it did not take.

It was a little bit like madness, attempting this. They had no prepared circle, no ritual. Nothing to bind with or pay by, not even the formula of a prayer or precedent. All they had was this place, the old cradle of a god still dripping with the afterbirth of its creation, and the sea of Gloam around them. What they sought to do, it was like striking a match atop gunpowder pot while riding a wild horse.

The flesh beneath their feet shuddered the third galleass fired, a wave of powder smoke streaking across water as the balls flew and lodged into the monster’s body. The same thing that had saved them earlier, the mold being in the way, was now preventing any of the ships from getting a clear shot at its skull to kill it. One of the balls overshot, hit the stone of the mold and chipped off a piece with a whistling sound.

“Mean it,” Maryam told her sister. “You have to mean it.”

She traced comfort on the veil, which had never felt thinner, and Hooks shivered.

“_Hear me_,” Hooks ordered the world, and this time it took heed.

Gloam and water shivered, then went still as stone. Held, seized.

“I was named and yoked to the tyranny under which I will labor, as is the charge of all living things,” Hooks said, then grit her teeth. “That is not enough. I claim a name of my own, a place in the chain of hierarchy.”

They drew in the Gloam, sucked in like a breath. Only this was not some casket in a crypt, surrounded by candles. This was the cradle of Scholomance, hidden inside its belly, and down here the dark dwelled deep. When Hooks called, the Gloam came in rivers. Torrents came from the sky and the sides, pouring in, and Maryam heard shouts and questions but could not spare the thought to parse them – every inch of her was needed to keep the Gloam from drowning them.

And from the mold, her sister drew out the afterbirth of Scholomance, that accursed lingering liquid. She stole it out on strands of Gloam, carefully picking out the liquid strands.

“I sacrifice three things,” Hooks said, teeth tight. “First, the remnants of a god’s name.”

There was a ripple in the water below, like a burst of wind.

“Second, the thwarting of a curse.”

Besides them, Song violently jerked. Her tormentor had heard that and not liked it at all. Before the third offering could be made, they had to reach out for the Gloam they’d drawn in. Shape it even as thunder echoed across the lake, as cannons tore into the ketos, as the curse-god behind Song finally pushed aside the last of keto’s mind and seized the body.

The beast was dying. With so many holes in it, it would drown if it perished again. Even if it did not, it would bleed out – its flanks were bloody, ragged ruins. The Western Fleet had done the work, but the last breath was still there to be snatched.
