It was a jagged, ugly spike they put together in the air above the monster, weaving even the strands of afterbirth inside, and when it was finished Maryam took her hand off. Left it entirely to her sister, who had to finish it on her own.

“Third, the death of a ketos,” Hooks swore, and slammed the spike into the monster’s open wound, seeking the heart.

And in the same moment, won thrice: she spent the last of the god’s name, thwarted the curse trying to murder Song and slew the ketos by punching roiling Gloam deep into the heart.

An offering promised and given in the same breath, rippling out into the aether, and Hooks seized the ripples desperately. Gathered them to her, every scrap she could until the ripple was dead and silence followed in its wake. The ketos was a floating carcass, the cannons had fallen silent, and around them the darkness slowly began to clear until they could see it.

In the distance, to the north, a small star. A distant shore, the path ahead.

“Ester,” she whispered. “My name is Ester.”

So she said, and she made it so.

 

# Chapter 62

They left the beast dead in the water, an island of flesh and horror drifting timelessly in the dark.

There was cheering, flares filled the sky in celebration. Someone was singing and backs were clapped. All of it washed over Tristan like water on wax. The business was not yet finished. He stayed in the tall cabin; someone began to climb to join him, then thought better of it. It took too long but the joy passed, swallowed by the dark bite by bite. The galleasses gathered to trail behind their ship, crows chasing the carrion yet to be.

North they all went, past the silent cradle of the god whose own innards they sailed, towards the distant star that was no such thing.

Tristan knew what would be waiting on that shore before they ever reached it. He could feel it: heat against his palm, a song in his ear. The same way he could feel Scolomancia’s hands at work around them, already refolding the school with patient meticulousness. How she prepared to tuck away the lake and the grand carcass somewhere beyond the reach of those who would come after them – the Watch would return here and find only a path to awaited ahead.

The star was no such thing: it was a high gate to what lay beyond.

They cut through the dark like a knife, Scolomancia’s hymn rising at the approach. Izel’s lantern did not gutter with the wind, barely even swung, and Tristan would have thought them trapped in a bubble of pale amber if not the destination taking shape before them.

The shrine was like the mouth of a womb. The black, flesh-like stone opened into a world of light: the opening had been the false-star, the light from beyond seeming like a source of its own instead of the spillover it truly was. It was taller than men, broader than them, and past the troubling mouth the stone turned intricate. Carved with signs, words and cryptoglyphs all woven together in knots so tangled as to be oppressive.

Up on his perch, he felt Scolomancia’s ice-cold breath against the back of his neck.

“Thus I Have Learned The Language Of All Living Things,” she rasped against his ear, leaning close.

Half the motto of this school, the same engraved on the brumal silver nestled against his heart. It didn’t burn when it touched his skin, he’d checked. Would check again. It was how he knew he was not yet beyond the point of no return.

“It that what it says?” he asked.

“Lesson,” Scolomancia rasped. “None Stand Beyond The Eldest Law.”

She stroked his hair almost tenderly, every touch was like hot coals. It burned under his skin, the searing stirred to life by her attentions. A man could tend to two shrines, Tristan thought, but he could not be priest twice over. Gods, from the greatest slaughter-swelled of Izcalli to the dustiest of Murk idols, where greedy things. They suffered not to share what they claimed. Tristan held the truth that the Father of Lies had whispered to him in the palm of his hand. Turned it over, studied it.

Put it away for now, back into the box.

Let there be mercy enough in the Circle’s spin that he need never test the truth of it, to find out if he could save it all by losing it all.

Scolomancia was gone a breath later, the burns lingering in her absence. He saw that on the deck below silver eyes had found him and almost smiled down at his captain. The goddess ever avoided Song’s gaze, hiding in the dead angles of it like a ghost haunting from corners. Tristan found little relief in that, not when Scolomancia now walked underneath his skin every moment he spent inside these walls. A lighthouse could not quell the night.

They made shore on a beach of black rubble, the fallen masonry polished like gems by the patient hands of time and water, and Tristan slipped past even the Skiritai to leap down into the shallows. He almost slipped on the wet stone but a hand steadied him – the tip of her fingers burned, _burned _like embers sown into the skin – and he let out a gasp. Let them think it was the coolness of the water, not the spots of skin next to his ribs he could _swear_ were charred black.

He was the first to the mouth of the shrine, but his steps slowed as he went up hacked-up slopes so gentle they might as well be stairs. There was a buzzing, Scolomancia’s tune trying and failing to drown it out as his eyes skimmed over the shapes of cryptoglyphs.

“A disquieting place.”

Tristan might have startled, were he still enough in his body for it. Instead he reacted only at a second of delay, long after the flash of surprise had thinned. He’d not heard Angharad approach but she was at his side now, boots water-slick and blade in hand.

“It talks, I am told, about the Eldest Law,” Tristan told her.

Sakkas had told him about it, once, the monster whose name the bird bore. _I should not have said that._ Secrets leaking out of him like a sieve. Holes were hollowing him out, making lace of him.

“And its name is extinction,” Angharad softly said.

This time he did startle, and so did Scolomancia as she rode him. The violin slipped. She had not expected this.

“How do you know that?” he said.

Angharad’s gaze was somewhere very far away even as it rested on the high gate.

“I was told so by the Fisher.”

Tristan cocked his head at the mention, wondering if Scolomancia would recognize the name, but there was nothing from her. Angharad shivered.

“He thinks little of this place,” she whispered. “I cannot tell whether that is glad news or a grim portent.”

“It can be a fine line, with gods,” Tristan said, and resumed the climb.

The light hit him like a wave, almost toppling him over. He blinked through the pain, steadying as he stepped onto solid stone and heard Angharad exhort the others to follow. She joined him in the shining pale, their footsteps echoing across a dusty nothing.

They stood hemmed in by stone on either side, Vesper’s true firmament spread above as the Grand Orrery’s false stars spun slowly.

They were at the bottom of a canyon. Ahead what could only be the Glass Repository sat astride a plateau, its grand glass dome and metal spites glittering like jewels. Even from this distance he could make out the endless, towering stacks – shelves piled up taller than castle walls, longer than streets, bound together by bridges so thin as to be artful. The problem was the road to get there.

Between the mouth of the shrine and the bottom of cliff stood and long, bare stone way. The slightly inclined slope on either side must be a hundred feet tall and half as wide, continuing straight for at least four hundred yards. At the end of the trench the path split on either side of a triangular bastion not quite as high as the sides, its flat stone roof bordered with toppled statues and loose masonry. There was no visible gate into the bastion – perhaps further down the split hallways – but past the tall ridge on either side he could see lifts rising up the cliffside.

And, hanging above the bastion, was the Machinist’s second creation.

The creature was almost as large as the fort below it, hanging off the cliff by eight spindly legs, and it had a spider’s cast but turned... wrong. The body was oddly proportioned, the spinneret larger than the rest of it put together. The thorax was oddly elongated and ended in a head shaped like a red bowl-crown with a protruding curl. The mouth beneath the ‘crown’ was long, in the form of a T with an almost oval hole above it, and it kept rattling a thousand teeth as it sucked in breaths.

That was not as unsettling as what was coming out of her spinneret, thick strands of something linen-like that slid all the way down to the back of the bastion where black-cloaked silhouettes pulled it out from some eldritch purpose.

The others caught up, footsteps interwoven, but one gait he picked out from the rest. Heavy but faintly apologetic about it.

“I don’t suppose you would know what that is, Izel?” he asked without turning.

The tinker was the finest among them when it came to teratology. He did not disappoint.

“I don’t know the name,” Izel replied, “but I’ve read of something like this. They dwell in the Desolation, west of the Kingdom of Jahamai, in great crypts buried by the ashen storms that sweep across the Anuja.”

There was a whistling sound, someone impressed and appalled and most of all nonchalant.

“Now_ that_ it is nasty bit of fortification,” Musa Shange mused. “How would one even go about assaulting it?”

Tristan was no general, but even a child could see it. Hundreds of yards of narrow open ground facing the enemy fortifications with nowhere to go but forward or back. A hundred men could hold that canyon against five times that, if they had enough powder. Did Cai Wei? For Tristan did not doubt for a moment that it was her revenants they glimpsed in the distance, moving like black-clad ants.

“-must be a way to flank that, the side corridors ought to lead somewhere that-”

He did not pay the impromptu tactics debate any mind. It wouldn’t matter, anyway: this was the path that Scolomancia would give them every time. The straight run at doom, death on a road of stone. He was on his third step before anyone noticed.

“Tristan?”

He flicked a glance back at Song, avoiding her eyes. He found it hard to look her in them, these days.

“Just taking a closer look,” he said, and angled his hat down.

That way he could no longer see the naked truth that she did not want him to go. That she would order him not to, were she not afraid he would ignore the order in front of cabalists from other brigades. That discomfort nipped at his heels but he outran it. He always outran it. _There is work_, he told himself, and sunk into the cold embrace of that comfort.

The stone was bare, but it was not uniform: it had been worn at by centuries of weather, leaving channels and impressions. None all that deep, but enough that a man might be able to move from one to another in the shade between the sweeps of the Orrery lights. Tristan went at it methodically, but without fear. Tucked behind every corner he could see corpse-lips smiling, the goddess crammed into blind angles, and he knew there would be no catching him as long a Scolomancia smiled on him.

A hundred yards in, she intervened. Pressed against stone, cheek on the cool and dusty surface, he moved to follow the darkening sweep only for a hand to lay against his cheek. He swallowed the scream, the certainty that his skin had curdled black and was flaking in the wind, and only moved when she let him. Scolomancia painted it for him, after that: like strokes of blood he could see where the gazes swept, where they lingered.

Humming along with the dirge – when had it begun? – Tristan slipped between the rivers of blood, from shadow to shadow, as distance was swallowed up. First he saw the cannons on the heights, pieces rustled up from half a dozen different epochs and crammed between cover of statues and debris. A hundred powder-mouths ready to belch out death at any comer. It was not enough. There was movement on the bastion, where the revenants pulled down the linen from the monster’s spinneret like a swarm of weavers.

What were they _doing_ with it?

He strode between two swiveling fields of blood, pivoting so that not even the hem of his cloak was caught, and calmly pressed himself into the stone’s cracks as a third swept over him. When he ducked out, stepped into the blind, he finally saw it: the revenants _were _weaving with the cloth. Fashioning the silhouettes of men and women then filling them. With meat, corpse parts, but also shovels of something Tristan was too far to discern._ Ash_, he guessed. It was what the revenants dissolved into when slain.

Almost there. Only a little further and he could make the run to slip into the dead angle at the foot of the bastion. From there he could explore the hallways, find out the paths. Gather the secrets he must provide to the garrison before it could begin to entertain an assault on this place.

A cold breath against his neck stopped him.

“Heavy,” Scolomancia rasped. “Give.”

It would have been a mercy to be able to misunderstand her, but he didn’t. The knowledge was in his brain, delivered by an iron spike of agony. Fortuna’s gift, the sacrifice she had made to save his life from the false dantesvara – the same boon Lady Knit had once coveted.

Scolomancia wanted him to be rid of it. To give it to her or, if not, to toss it away.

“It’s why I burn, isn’t it?” he whispered. “When you touch me. It’s stopping me from becoming your priest."

"_Heavy_," Scolomancia hissed.

And he would be lightfooted, if he threw it away. Enough that he would be able to slither past the gazes of the revenants, to dig out the secrets and open the way. He could almost taste the boon. All he needed to do was throw away Fortuna’s gift and he’d have the strength, the swiftness. The goddess in the walls promised all this and more. Tristan’s hand reached for a coin to flip but seized with pain. His bones ground and his flesh burned. He flinched, stopping, and hated himself for it.

“There must be something else,” he said.

Her silence was the only answer.

Of course there was. But this was the price she wanted him to pay.

It was worse when you knew it was coming, but Tristan did it anyway. His fingers clenched around nothing as he swallowed a scream, felt out where a coin that’d never been would be. The pain was atrocious, and did not flow into some distant sense of agony – it was there, sharp and whole for every moment. And still Tristan held it, releasing only in his own time. His brow felt feverish, his back covered with sweat.

“No,” Tristan told her. “’It’s mine.”

He had expected a tantrum. Hot pokers thrust between his ribs, fingernails ripped out. Screams in violin, shifting ground. Instead what Tristan got was complete, utter silence.

She was gone.

Scolomancia was gone and, he dimly realized as he emerged from his trance, he was now more than two hundred yards deep into a trench of bare stone that revenants watched every inch of like hawks. He stood there paralyzed, pressed into the crack, struck dumb by the absurdity of his position. He was wondering whether it would be courage or madness to muster up the will to begin the trek back when the choice was made for him.

There was a shout from the heights, the glint of Orrery light on steel and a shot resounded. He threw himself to the ground, in time for stone shards to splatter against his cloak, and crawled back up to _run_. Run like a rabbit, like a fool, like someone behind whom Hell had opened its gates. And Hell screamed: arquebuses, muskets even a small cannon spraying shrapnel he felt tear into the back of his shoulder.

Shouts from ahead, someone running towards him as he stumbled.

There was a sharp crack, a rifle, and all that Tristan had the time to feel was_ pain_ before it all-

--

Even in his sleep he looked afraid, Song thought.

The physicians had twice asked her to order Tristan to take the sedatives, that they might dig out the musket ball out of him without needing to strap him down, but she’d refused. It was his choice, even if hearing him scream as they cut him open had been like nails on slate. He’d eventually passed out from the pain and exhaustion, tucked away in his little room, and Song had remained. She had a book to stare at without reading and the time to spare to wonder how much of this was on her.

Maryam was sleeping in the corner, bundled up in a chair with cloaks and blankets, but her sister was still awake and pacing back and forth across the room. Soundlessly: the newly-named Ester Khaimov seemed possessed with a boundless energy, but she was not so selfish as to keep her battered sister from her rest. The younger Khaimov looked different, now.

She did not change her shape as much as she had before, and not as quickly or easily – there was a base now, something she was moving away _from_. And where Song had once found a faint translucence to her, an etherealness, there was now solidity. By taking on a name, Ester had become more... grounded. Real, in a metaphysical sense. She was now less an aether intellect on a leash and more a fully formed soul.

The sharpness of her face had lightened some but it remained more angular than Maryam’s, her eyes a deeper blue and her height taller by at least two inches. There were rings around her eyes now, though, and somehow Song did not think she was the one who’d put them there. _There is a price to everything._ In putting on a name Ester had become closer to alive, but to be alive meant to cease being a creature of pure thought.

“Am I finally more interesting than your book?” Ester asked.

Song grimaced, conceding defeat by closing it shut.

“I cannot seem to focus on the pages,” she admitted.

Both their gazes dipped to the source of her distraction, Tristan’s prone body on the bed. He did not turn or toss, bandaged too tightly to easily turn, and the paleness to his face had him looking half a corpse. His locks were still sweat-soaked, his face seemingly never more than a breath away from flinching.

“He’s the one who chose to try that approach,” Ester said, then bit her lip. “No one forced him, no one even asked.”

“No,” Song softly agreed. “But I let him do it.”

Her fingers clenched.

“Because he always pulls through, always delivers, I let him walk into what we could all see was madness.”

The way she had let him chase Cao’s trail until exhaustion broke him down. It was so easy to trade away his time, his efforts – he never complained, so long as he saw the sense in the bargain, and so often they saw eye to eye about what needed to be done. _He was the copper there for easy spending, and so I thoughtlessly spent him._

“Some might call that trust,” Ester said.

“Then the weight of my trust has put him in a hospital bed,” Song replied through gritted teeth.

She should have known better. Scolomancia was getting to him, she’d known that. And he’d already worked himself so hard that he had collapsed mere days ago, he had been riding ragged edge for weeks. But she’d let him keep pushing a little further every time because he always made it worth it. Just another member of her brigade she was using, like she had used Maryam as cover to selfishly pursue the delve. Only instead of nearly deserting as she suspected the Khaimovs had, Tristan had talked himself into one bold folly too many and gotten shot for it.

Twice, if you counted the shrapnel separately from the bullet. Song did, since if that old cannon had been aimed half an inch to the left most of Tristan Abrascal’s innards would have been shredded and he would not have lived long enough for Angharad to drag him back to the ship. The way the taste of victory had curdled in her mouth, replaced by a pounding terror as they fled back across the lake and down the coast to the hospital, it was a memory that would long stay with her. It _should_.

“I’ve asked too much of him,” she finally said.

“We all did,” Ester said. “Except for Angharad. Funny how that goes, isn’t it? At the start of the year he hardly trusted her.”

Song was not sure that was true. Or rather it only was if you thought of trust as the Khaimov sisters often did, some sort of merciless absolute. Tristan had trusted Angharad over_ some_ matters, simply not all of them. The two Izvorica simply did not deign to consider something so conditional worthy of the word. A knock on the door had them both tensing, Song rising to crack it open.

One of the gray-robed physicians waited on the other side, though the man was not only that: tattooed against the side of his neck was a knot of gray string, Lady Knit’s mark. He was a priest as well.

“Captain Ren,” the man said, inclining his head. “Is the patient awake?”

“He is not.”

“Unfortunate,” the man said, in a tone belying the word. “This my lady’s only available moment for some time. Are you willing to wake him for such an audience?”

Her eyes narrowed at the priestling. Was Lady Knit was trying to avoid offering Tristan a bargain? It would not work, not even if Song had to stay overnight to ensure the goddess was ushered into the room the very moment he next woke.

“I am not,” she said. “I will fetch one of your fellows the moment he is with us again.”

“As you say,” the man said, inclining his head. “Pleasant vigil, captain.”

She did not return the courtesy, only closing the door in his face. Ester was scowling through the wall at the man when she turned.

“He got on Knit’s bad side after Misery Square,” Ester said. “She’s going to try and gouge him on the price.”

“I am aware,” Song said. “But she is under oath to the Watch to keep her prices fair.”

“Fair for who?” Ester replied. “If you lost a leg, would you call it fair to get it back for the price of forswearing the Repository?"

Song grimaced. A leg was no small thing, but to never step foot in the Glass Repository might well mean her sister’s death. She grasped the implication, plain as it was.

“You think she has this sort of offer for Tristan?”

“Fortuna left something on him,” Ester said. “She’ll ask for that, mark my words.”

And Tristan would refuse, because to surrender even the slightest part of Fortuna while she was fading away just out of his reach would be more than he could suffer. She almost cursed. That meant he would not be back on his feet tomorrow but be left to recuperate for weeks before he was fit to be anywhere near combat. _It will drive him mad, or worse._

Another knock on the door killed what she’d been about to say, Song’s brow pulling into a frown as she eyed the door. Surely the priest was not back?

“Ah,” Ester muttered. “You’ll want to take this one alone.”

She was gone in an instant, there and then not, and Song put on a calm face as she cracked open the door again. Immediately a foot was wedged in and Colonel Chunhua Cao pushed through without a word, jostling Song as she eyed the room just long enough to choose a chair by the wall. Cao then turned an expectant look on Song, as if exhorting her to close the door like a proper servant, and tugged at her collar before sitting.

_Hand on the chisel_. Song closed the door.

“Colonel,” she brusquely said. “This is a surprise.”

“No,” Chunhua Cao said. “It isn’t. Such a conversation has been some time in the making. What _is _a surprise is that you managed to pull in the Western Fleet and get us to the gates of the Repository.”

“I am no longer a member of the delve,” Song said, folding her hands behind her back. “There is no _us_, ma’am.”

Colonel Cao crossed her legs, leaning back into the seat.

“Would you like to be?” she casually asked.

“Pardon?”

“A member of the delve,” Cao said. “It can be arranged easily enough.”

Her lips thinned. And hand over the fruits of the Thirteenth’s efforts so that Cao could use them to secure her coup? Even were it not a betrayal of Colonel Azocar the thought would be distasteful.

“A generous offer,” she said. “I must consult my bri-”

“Your brigade is falling apart,” Cao said. “You’ve led them into too many breaches, Song. Several months of combat and exploration is not unusual in certain parts of the Watch, but such a pace is the province of veterans.”

The colonel cocked her head to the side.

“Life has hardened your cabalists, but it does not make them career soldiers,” Cao said. “It is quite plain to anyone looking that your brigade must either slow down or splinter.”

Song’s hand slipped.

“That would be convenient for you, wouldn’t it?”

She cursed herself, fingers tightening against the chisel until they turned bloodless. There was nothing to gain here by losing her temper.

“It doesn’t really matter,” Colonel Cao calmly replied. “I’m not unaware that I used too much the stick with you, Song, but this... delusion of us being adversaries does not survive in the glare of day.”

A brow was arched.

“You are, at this point, largely irrelevant,” she said. “A bastion like that will need a mass assault to be taken, or a months-long siege, and thus you cannot deliver to Colonel Azocar the Repository. That was the only bullet in your pistol – there is, frankly, nothing else you can do that would weigh on the scales of my career.”

“If that’s true,” Song said, “then why are you here?”

“Because, while you proved to be overly emotional in your decision-making, you’ve also proved capable of captaining an extremely capable cabal,” Cao said. “I mishandled the situation with Morcant, and it would be wasteful to snuff out the career of someone with your promise.”

Song studied her for a long moment.

“You’re lying.”

“I don’t need to,” Cao gently said. “I under-”

“No, not that part,” Song said. “Maybe you believe that, but it’s not why you’re here. There’s something else.”

Silver eyes narrowed.

“Has the Krypteia paid you a visit?”

Cao laughed.

“Are you so important that your tantrum would warrant the attention of the Masks, Song?”

_No. But it doesn’t matter, because that’s the laugh of someone who just lied._ Something had Cao spooked, had her wanting to bring Song back onto the poisonous fold instead of strangling her and tossing the corpse of her career out on the street for everyone to see. Only Song had no idea what it was.

“I will make it easy for you,” Colonel Cao said. “There are two paths ahead of you now. The first, the path of reason, is the one where you resume a place of honor among the leading Stripes of your year, joining the delve again just before it is disbanded and turned into an official Watch operation. When the Repository is secured, I will ensure you have access to the Book of the Lofty Mountain should it be in the stacks.”

Cao’s legs uncrossed.

“The second is the path where you stubbornly cling to Fermin and your one-sided grudge, leaving me no choice but to make an example of you,” she continued, rising to her feet.

She closed the distance, coming to stand over Song.

“One of the many, many irregularities the Thirteenth was involved in will be brought to the attention of the Obscure Committee, you will be expelled from this school and the only copy of that book you might feasibly reach is permanently barred to you.”

Cao stared her down.

“You have until the delve is disbanded,” she said. “Let that day pass without first visiting me at the Galleries and I will take it to mean there is no coming to terms with you.”

They matched gazes, eye to eye, until Cao had found whatever it was she was looking for. The colonel walked out of the room without a backwards glance back, leaving Song to stand there in silence. And there she stood, considering the threat. The words spoken, but also those not. After a long time Ester slipped out of her sister and came to stand besides her, staring at the same closed door.

“Why are you smiling?” Ester finally asked. “That was an ultimatum.”

“Because she came to give it at all,” Song said. “And that means that Tristan was wrong – there’s still something on this island that she’s afraid we’ll find.”

And best they find it soon, else whatever had Cao feeling safe enough to make that threat would come to pass.

--

Izel did not consider himself a man of slow thought, but the last few days had moved dizzyingly quick to him.

The aftermath of the second passage through the lake had been... tumultuous. The redemption of the Thirteenth’s reputation he had hoped for never came to pass, as hardly any townsfolk had known of the ketos as more than a rumor and none had felt threatened by it. Still, the discovery of the last redoubt of the traitor Cai Wei and her revenants made some waves. There was a sense of light on the horizon, which improved the mood in town – if not enough to make up for losing one’s home and possessions.

Among students the slaying of the ketos had been met with accolades, though deservedly a great deal of the honor was shared with the three well-armed galleasses sent by the Western Fleet. They and the ranks of the local garrison were alight with talk of when the bastion would be assaulted, the fearsome defenses contrasted with how close the Watch was to reaching the Repository and being able to slay the Machinist.

Those that made it best out of the whole affair were the sailors. The flotilla from the Western Fleet had decisively slain a monster within a week of arriving and the influx of sailors with coin to burn had been popular with the townsfolk. It helped that the armed contingents from the galleons and the many cannons resting in Allazei Bay lent much-needed aid to the fading sense of safety.

The Thirteenth had not wasted its time. It’d been six days since the ketos was slain and Izel had spent most of them inside the Workshop when he was not attending class or visiting the hospital. Now that he was free to sell aether spike dispensers – _blastcaps_, what a stupid name – he’d struck deals with several leading brigades and was busy digging his finances out of the hole he’d dug for them. The First, the Ninth and Third had all paid for either a dispenser or the plans for it so he’d even avoided dragging the Unluckies into brigade squabbles.

Song was busying herself with correspondence and plots with other Stripes, not the least of them Ferranda Villazur. The captain of the Thirty-First’s meetings with all the brigades at the bottom of the Stripe rankings were beginning to draw some attention. Maryam had been in and out of meetings with the Western Fleet for days, arranging the last details of her bargain with them, and Hooks – Ester now, he reminded himself – was buzzing around with seemingly endless enthusiasm.

Angharad was even braving Captain Wen’s suggestion of staying out of town by having arranged meetings for Acallar hunts that were well attended, though she let Lindiwe Sarru lead them in her stead. The stares that had her wilting were far from gone, but with every day she was seen in the Dregs or the Crocodilians with a full table of fellow Skiritai the hostility grew a little more hesitant. The Militants tended to get a different tone of respect from the townsfolk than other covenanters, and seeing them openly refusing to shun her was denting the tide.

Only so much, though, so Izel usually made sure to stick with her just as she did with him when he had Workshop hours running long. He’d settled on a neighboring table with his back to the wall, a cup of cider and a treatise on the preponderance of prime numbers in aether tinkering and the possible connections to First Empire cryptoglyphs, but he was barely halfway through when the rowdy talks audibly began to wind down.

He spared a look at the assembled dozen – Lindiwe Sarru’s allies and Angharad’s as well as a few spares attracted by the prospect of glory – and found the usual at play. Sarru looked smug, pleased and smugly pleased. Having Angharad in her Acallar crew had been a coup and she kept rubbing it in everyone’s face. Angharad was taking it well enough, but as Izel watched her quietly talking with a tight-jawed Shalini he noted, not for the first time, that not everyone was so sanguine about it.

It didn’t help that Sarru kept taunting Shalini about it.

Closing the booklet, he drained the last dregs of his cider cup and rose to his feet.

“-know you want her help to deal with Wei, but she is being _odious_,” Shalini was harshly whispering.

Ah, Izel thought. That. The second reason for their little gathering, the one that had proved admirably sneaky on Angharad’s part. With all those Militants already gathered at the table, she had ventured the idea that since Cai Wei was a Skiritai Guild deserter from their year she could be said to be their batch’s duty to deal with. The idea had been popular with those inclined to chase glory, and not outright refused by most of the rest.

No one had forgotten Wei’s last raid into town and the damage it’d done.

“It is only for a few months still,” Angharad tried to reassure.

Shalini clenched her teeth, then shook her head.

“A few months too many,” she said, and walked away.

It felt almost unkind to come to stand by Angharad after that, the mirror-dancer planted there and watching her angry lover leaving. Izel spared her a few moments, then cleared his throat.

“If we get moving soon, we can catch Maryam on her way back from port,” he said.

Angharad coughed.

“Yes,” she managed. “Let’s.”

He did not dare venture any romantic advice. Izel certainly wasn’t doing well enough in that quarter to be handing it out. They went for the door, which opened before Izel could push it out – and he stopped in surprise as the sight of Professor Achari. He’d never seen the older man in the Crocodilian before.

“Ah, my boy,” Achari said. “It seems I caught you just in time. May I have a word?”

He flicked a look at Angharad, who seemed only amused. She gestured a vague approximation of ‘only fair’ and they both drew back to let in the professor.

“In private would be best,” Achari said.

Something about the professor’s expression has his stomach clenching up. They took a corner table, as private as one could get without paying for a room, and Professor Achari sat down. The older man stroked his beard with an uneasy air.

“I have received word from a friend abroad,” he said, wasting no time on small talk. “An officer from one of the workshops on Khalkea is soon to file for a patent for a device that might be familiar to you.”

The professor handed him a rough charcoal sketch on paper, Izel’s heart clenching at the sight. It wasn’t a lenslight, not exactly. The basic parts were there - a source of Glare, a fuel chamber, an aether-forged lens – but they were assembled differently. The Glare kernel was much closer to the lens, the fuel chamber larger and to the back while the containment mirrors fed directly into the mouth of the device. It was shaped more like a gourd than a box.

At a guess, it would be better than his own design at strengthening the power of the Glare in a narrow beam but lack the ability to emit more broadly. _I made a light, this is a lance._ It was his idea made into what could only be called a weapon.

“This is theft,” Izel flatly said. “Open, brazen theft.”

“Brazen, yes,” Professor Achari soberly said. “But theft? You never patented the device, my boy. They are attempting to steal a march on you in that regard.”

“I have dated evidence I worked on it long before they thought to petition for their patent,” Izel insisted.

“And they will claim they came to the notion independently,” Achari told him. “If neither side can come to an agreement-”

He raised a questioning eyebrow here and Izel sharply shook his head.

“-then the matter will be put to the Wednesday Council’s adjudication,” the older man finished.

“Which will rule for me, given the evidence,” Izel slowly said. “The simple fact that my chest was broken into and then the device mysteriously appeared elsewhere weeks later should be enough to have this officer imprisoned.”

Achari’s lips thinned. He did not answer.

“You cannot be serious,” Izel said, disbelieving. “Such blatant corruption would savage their reputation, what tinker would trust them to be fair afterwards?”

“To grant you the patent and deny it to Khalkea would mean examining the device,” Professor Achari said. “The council will side with you, I expect, but given the potential usefulness of the machine they may be pressured by other parts of the Watch to make a compromise ruling.”

Izel swallowed.

“Who?”

“The name was carefully kept out,” Achari said, “but the Khalkea workshop took up the matter on behalf of another, the second-in-command of Lucierna weapons workshop.”

It took him a moment to recall.

“Helena’s father,” he quietly said.

“Lieutenant Ulises Vargas,” Achari confirmed. “Their family has connections in Khalkea, which he now uses as a catspaw. But should the device prove promising enough, I expect Marshal Camaron himself will get involved. It would be quite the feather in his cap to have the workshop producing these under his authority.”

“She’s the one who broke into my chest, then,” Izel hoarsely said.

“There is no proof,” Achari said, but nothing more than that.

“Can Camaron really force the matter?” Izel desperately asked. “He is the head of a Garrison region, but hardly the only one. Could he really pressure the Umuthi Society to bend?”

“Alone, hardly,” Achari said. “But he has friends in high places who would be quite interested in the potential of the lenslight as a weapon should it prove effective. It might be some time before that proof can be secured, though.”

Izel thought, then, of Musa Shange on the deck of their skimmer. Of his nonchalant asking about the lenslight, about the oddity of him having used a favor for the right to join the battle against the ketos_. He wasn’t here for the fight_, Izel thought. _He was there to find out for Marshal Camaron if the lenslight is worth the squabble to secure._

“No,” he softly said. “I expect word about it is already sailing back to Lucierna as we speak. My window is closing.”

He would need to patent it today, this very hour, and hope to the gods that the Thirteenth came out of the final push for the Repository with favors to call in.

Else it looked like his work was about to be let loose on the world.

 

# Chapter 63

Izel waited until evening, after the others had gone to bed. Song did not need to be told that they must talk, making time and tea without prompting. He returned the courtesy by refraining from wasting time or measuring his words when telling her about the situation. He laid it all out.

How the patent for the lenslight would soon be contested by a workshop on Khalkea, the face of it a sergeant by the name of Garci Calvo. That Professor Achari had been told it was a front and Lieutenant Ulyses Vargas was behind it. How the latter man was the father of Helena Vargas, the tinker he believed to have sent lenslight plans, and also the head of the Lucierna weapons workshop. How Izel now believed that Musa Shange had been ordered to join the battle against the ketos to ascertain for Marshal Camaron whether the lenslight was worth the bureaucratic fight to secure.

When he’d finished, Song sipped calmly at her tea and set it down with tightly controlled evenness

“I must confess I am not conversant in the process of disputes over Watch patents,” Song said, sounding like a woman already planning to remedy that. “What will it look like?”

Izel had not been all that familiar himself. It was not encouraged for tinkers to get quarrelsome with each other. Professor Achari had known, though, and freely shared.

“It depends on who the disputing parties are,” Izel said. “In this case, the sergeant on Khalkea that will be disputing the patent is also of the Umuthi Society so it will be a society tribunal.”

He paused, gathering his thoughts.

“Since we’re not part of the same workshop or command, where a higher-ranked tinker could settle the matter, it will be kicked up directly to the Wednesday Council,” he said. “Normally they would appoint someone to handle it for them, but this case is important enough they might elect one of their own instead.”

Or so Achari believed, anyway. He’d been of the opinion that even had the lenslight not sparked interest the involvement of Marshal Camaron behind the scenes would have guaranteed the Wednesday Council would pay close attention to the dispute.

“And this adjudicator will have full authority to decide on the matter?” Song asked.

“Yes and no,” Izel hedged. “First there’ll be a hearing to state the cases, to make sure neither is so egregious it can be outright dismissed, then if there can be no cordial resolution they call for a full tribunal. And even after that tribunal gives their verdict, either side can still appeal the decision to the Conclave if they believe there was something unjust or corrupt about the process.”

Song’s brow rose.

“_Directly_ to the Conclave?”

Izel smiled wanly.

“You noticed it fast,” he said. “Yes, it’s to the general assembly so there’s no guarantee that the petition will be added to the next docket. And even if it is, there’s no guarantee it will be tabled for a vote that same session. It could stay pending for months or even years.”

Professor Achari had frankly told him that this was occasionally used as a way to bury cases that would cause unrest within Watch ranks until the worst of tempers had cooled.

“And what happens to the patent while the appeal is pending?” Song asked.

She’d been taught by a colonel based on the Rookery, hadn’t she? Her uncle Zhuge. It showed: she kept homing in on the right details.

“Production is suspended, but making models for research purposes is still allowed,” Izel grimaced. “Which would be bad for me, Song.”

Because should a prototype be built in Khalkea and sent out for field testing then achieve something impressive, pressure would mount for the patent to be awarded to the Khalkean workshop. After all only one of the claimants was capable of establishing a production chain to make these on a large scale, or for that matter willing.

“You believe that getting a buried petition will be their plan,” Song said.

He nodded.

“Camaron can’t bully the Umuthi Society into doing what he wants,” he said. “So to prevent them bullying _him_, he’ll bring a flock of high-ranking officers at the hearing to warn off the Wednesday Council. Then he’ll push the matter into becoming a pending Conclave petition and keep it there until field test results and favors have secured him a voting majority.”

“And then he finally has the petition tabled,” Song murmured.

Izel nodded, then cleared his throat.

“Your uncle on the Rookery, do you think he could help?” he asked. “A peremptory dismissal of the petition would kill the appeal, kicking the matter back to the Umuthi Society.”

Who Professor Achari expected to side with him. Izel had expected a thoughtful look out of Song, or perhaps even some satisfaction at there being a clear path to ending the matter. Instead what he got was Song Ren’s fingers closing around the rim of her cup of tea as if she were trying to leech away some of the warmth. She was silent for a long moment and did not break her silence in the way he had expected.

“Conclave politics can be split into two broad camps,” Song abruptly said. “Philosophically speaking, I mean. There are dozens of factions and voting blocks over particular interests – taxation, expansion and isolation, harder or more accommodating lines of diplomacy – but typically these factions will broadly fall into one camp, save for temporary voting blocs over a single matter that draw members from both camps before collapsing.”

She paused.

“That is not to say those camps cover the entire Conclave ranks, or that they command voting majorities,” she said. “There are swaths of votes best described as unaligned opportunists or limited interests. Still, the dominant political currents in the Watch of our time are the opposing answers to a single question: should authority in the order centralize, or should it devolve?”

That was not an unfamiliar tune to him. The Calendar Court against the Sunflower Lords, the Maharaja against lesser kings and leagues. He was even vaguely familiar with the Watch’s own version of the pull between the heartlands and the regions.

“The Garrison against free companies,” he summed up.

“It is not that simple,” Song said, shaking her head. “You might be surprised to hear that some of the largest free companies are ardently in favor of the Conclave creating offices meant for more direct rule, so long as they are guaranteed seats. Meanwhile, some regional Garrison commanders are just as ardently against consolidation since it would cut into their independence and authority.”

She paused.

“Those against centralization are generally called ‘charterists’, as their most basic legal argument is based on the original charters the Watch was founded on,” Song said. “Those who are in favor of centralization are usually called ‘monocrats’, a word that means the advocacy of rule by one. That is because their leading political project is achieving the election of a Grand Marshal who could push through their desired reforms.”

“Marshal Camaron is the head of a strong regional command,” Izel slowly said. “So he is a charterist?”

She shook her head.

“He is actually one of the leading lights of the monocrats,” Song said. “I know this mostly because my uncle has monocrat sympathies himself – though he does not wear them openly, as that is unwise in a Rookery officer.”

She looked a little sick.

“I tell you this because it means that many of my uncle’s closest allies are monocrats,” Song said. “Marshal Camaron will also be a friend to several, and openly of their party besides. They are likely to side with him instead, and should Uncle Zhuge muster his charterist acquaintances instead the conflict becomes... unpredictable.”

Izel’s lips thinned.

“Because it’ll become charterists against monocrats, and at that point it doesn’t matter what the petition is actually about: they’ll both pour coin and influence into it just to thwart the other faction.”

She nodded.

“So there’s nothing we can do to stop them,” Izel said, swallowing drily. “Because they have allies up high and we do not.”

He paused. There was one friendly officer they’d met.

“Admiral Zokufa,” he said. “Do you think...”

She shook her head.

“He is no ally of Camaron’s, but the admiralty faction in the Conclave is a voting bloc that stays out of most politics,” Song said.

To be able to play both sides, Izel guessed. The monocrats would be in favor of funding the fleets because they were an arm of the Garrison, while the charterists would back the admiralty’s relative independence in the face of the Conclave to ensure no such fleet was ever used against them. _But it means they can’t afford to offend either side over small matters._

“Is there no one we can appeal to?” Izel asked, throat tight. “There must be someone who will look at this theft and be willing to do _something_ about it.”

He knew, objectively, that in this matter the Watch was still a cut above the other great powers. In Izcalli, if a great lord wanted something he had built and a greater lord did not protect him then the choice was between acquiescence and the grave. In Malan he would simply be forced by law to sell, the noble making a show of the generous payment offered no matter that he’d not wanted to be paid at all, while in Tianxia great trading cartels would simply blacklist and bankrupt him to force a sale.

That in the Watch this theft would be worked against by those in power, take years of gathered influence to accomplish and would still likely tarnish the reputation of the thieves for life... well, it did not make them good but it made them better than most.

Izel tried to tell himself that, but it was hard to believe it when choking on dark, impotent anger.

“This is on my head.”

His eyes swiveled back to Song. He was given physical pause by the absence of composure on her face. It didn’t last long, but the flash or rage fading into self-loathing struck him like a fist. Izel knew what those looked like; he saw them in the mirror often enough. Song rose to her feet, and to his horror began to bow. One of those waist-low Tianxi formal things. He caught her shoulder.

“Don’t,” he rasped. “That only makes it worse.”

“I am the one who pushed you to reveal the lenslight,” Song said. “Had it never been used, Marshal Camaron might not have deemed it worth the fight.”

“Plans of it had already been sent off,” Izel said. “It would have happened anyway, sooner or later.”

“But not like this,” Song tightly said. “It is on me to mend this, Izel. And I will do all I can.”

He grimaced. Kind words, but what could a student captain on Tolomontera really do against a marshal? She read it on his face.

“I can write to the Obscure Committee, at least,” Song darkly said. “Fenhua He should be no admirer of ours, but theirs is still the College seat at the table. I hold no great expectations for Lord Asher or Brigadier Laghari, but we might be able to garner the support of-”

She paused.

“Izel,” Song said. “I need you to test something with the lenslight.”

He cocked his head to the side.

“Why?”

“So I can write a letter,” Song Ren said.

And there was a gleam in those silver eyes, Izel thought, that reminded him of nothing so much as a sword.

--

It was turning out to be a pleasant night in a year that had counted too few of them.

Old Horvat – Angharad had thought it rude to call him this, but the man insisted – had found what he called ‘an almost passable brew, if the brewed by a one-armed blind lackwit’, which was apparently the highest compliment he had paid any beer since coming to Tolomontera. He’d invited the Thirteenth to try it, and Angharad had been intrigued enough to be among those who took him up on it when Maryam passed along the invitation.

It turned out to be a millet beer. Dark, malty and quite light in texture. It was from Dragada in the Someshwar, and quite unlike the millet beers from Uthukile that Angharad knew from back home – those were pale and thick instead, sold in traditional calabash gourds. Old Horvat’s find was also rather strong, which was why a _very _drunk Izel was currently dancing with Ester as Poltava and Young Koval valiantly tried to show them the steps to the tune the elder Koval was playing on the flute, a laughing Captain Wen slapping the table in accompaniment.

Orel Bolic had all but fled Angharad’s company after she politely inquired how the free knights of Zarla’s Drift had paid to maintain their arms and ships, muttering something about ‘fishing out treasures’ before finding a sudden and pressing need to help Old Horvat with the drinks.

That man, Angharad thought, had most _definitely _been a pirate.

The third tankard had her feeling a little hot around the collar, so when she saw Maryam slipping out in the courtyard she took the opportunity to follow her and take a breather in the cool night air. You almost couldn’t smell the smoke on the wind, these days. The rain had helped.

Her friend stayed close to the door, though out of the light, in deference to the lasting unpopularity of the Unluckies in town. Since the altercation at the market they all moved in pairs and avoided side streets.It would have driven Tristan mad, were he still on his feet. The Sacromontan was almost magnetically attracted to suspicious back alleys.

“Feeling the drink?” Angharad asked, joining her on the grass.

Maryam chuckled, shaking her head.

“It’s the noise and heat,” she said. “I get headaches. I’ve always been this way. I was not glad when my father had feasts either, even if the food almost made up for it.”

“I loved a good ball, myself,” Angharad wistfully said. “I missed quite a few for the dueling circuit – the society seasons in Peredur and Malan are not the same, so the tournament dates were an impediment – but those I attended were almost universally lovely.”

Maryam eyed her.

“Well, you’re,” she gestured at the whole of Angharad. “While I’m...”

She gestured at herself.

“I don’t follow,” Angharad admitted.

“We are built differently,” Maryam said, in the voice of someone who had just made a diplomatic decision. "Besides, practice of the Craft tends to instill a fondness for silence and solitude. It is the same with Navigators.”

It was an impulse to ask and she feared to be rude, so she held back. Not quickly enough to avoid notice, though.

“Ask,” Maryam said.

“I do not-”

“If I think it was rude, I’ll tell you as much,” her friend said.

Angharad cleared her throat.

“Did you ever regret it?” she asked. “Choosing to become a craftswoman instead of a princess. Many highborn would have balked at the choice.”

Herself among them.

“I was to be my mother’s apprentice and she was one of the Ninefold Nine, so I didn’t lose as much as you might think,” Maryam said. “Besides, my father still hosted us for a month or two every year and he made a point of giving us public and lavish gifts. Otherwise his rivals might think he could no longer call on my mother’s Craft should he be challenged.”

She _had_ mentioned her parents married largely for politics. Her mother had needed coin and support, her father the ties to a fearsome witch. The arrangement sounded like it had been cordial, which for some matches was the best one could hope for.

“But you went from a princess living in a court to a witch wandering the wilds and woods,” Angharad insisted. “You set aside a life of power and luxury to follow your duty.”

Maryam looked surprised.

“I didn’t see it as a duty,” she said. “Just a path. It only became something like duty when I was one of the last practitioners, when there was suddenly a tradition to preserve.”

“I am not sure I would have made the same choice in your place,” Angharad freely admitted. “I fought joining the Watch as long as I could even when my uncle urged otherwise, and after I put on the black I still clung to old trappings.”

The last society evenings left to her, the informal noble circle of Allazei. She had been more concerned with being at those dinners than what was being said during them.

“I’m not one to cast stones about holding on to one’s past,” Maryam said, glancing at the lit door and the musing drifting through it. “But this doesn’t sound like a fresh thought. What brought this on?”

Angharad folded her knees, lay her back against the wall.

“I suppose I am trying to understand why,” she said.

“Why?”

“Why someone would choose to side with the Machinist over the Watch,” Angharad said. “I have found I often make selfish choices when pressed, Maryam, so I thought to get insight from you – who so often sacrifices for duty and principle. You must have a different perspective.”

Maryam choked.

“Excuse me?”

“You chose your sister’s life over the ability to use Signs, Maryam,” Angharad reminded her. “And you chose your duty to your countrymen over ease, coin and almost your closeness to Tristan. Of us all I think you most often choose principle at your own expense.”

She was red in the cheeks. Had she truly not noticed?

“Izel,” she choked out.

“Izel broke an oath of betrothal and ran, then schemed to seize and sell a man to repay his debt to the Ivory Library,” Angharad flatly said. “He is my friend, and I respect his ideals, but he most often lives up to them when it is comfortable. You hold the same ember when it is still red.”

Maryam closed her eyes, face still red.

“I am going to pretend you never said that, and that I never heard it,” she announced. “We’ve had a few drinks. And you don’t know how close I came to making the wrong choice, Angharad. If it hadn’t been Ester,  I’m not sure I would have. So I suppose I _can_ understand where she comes from, Cai Wei.”

Angharad decided not fight the first half of that. Simpler to outright ignore it, and agree to nothing.

“I am relieved to hear you can,” Angharad said, leaning in. “How could she find the Machinist worth fighting for?”

She could see nothing honorable about his cause, nothing that made it worth taking up his banner. It was not as if the spirit were trying to restore the Kingdom of Sologuer, and he did not appear to be founding a cult either.

“She doesn’t give a shit about the Machinist,” Maryam said. “She’s afraid to die, Angharad.”

She blinked.

“We all are,” Angharad carefully said. “It does-”

“No, not like that you aren’t,” Maryam disagreed. “Becaus she doesn’t find any of it worth dying for, Angharad.”

Her friend gestured around them.

“The oaths, the school, the promises and the coin,” she said. “Your Skiritai rites down below. The Watch as whole – she cares about it less than she does about living. None of it is worth dying to honor, in her eyes, and to be honest I’m not sure she’s wrong.”

“You can’t mean that,” Angharad said, appalled.

“Not that we should fight for the Machinist instead,” Maryam dismissed. “But the way you described it, the Marshal tried to shoot her in the head the moment he could and she had decent odds of getting executed if she came back to the Watch. So she didn’t come back, and the Machinist was offering so she took up with him instead..”

“_Him_ is a monstrous god that butchered many of us with his works,” Angharad harshly said.

“How long was she really here, before she became a ghost?” Maryam asked. “A few weeks, a month or two? She didn’t buy into this place, probably not even into her old brigade. She had no reason to care about Scholomance or any of us.”

Her friend paused.

“She’s a villain to you,” Maryam said. “And I won’t say that it isn’t entirely deserved. But when you tell me about Cai Wei, Angharad, I’m left to wonder too.”

Eyes looked up at the colored Orrery stars, one dead and the other not. A price paid for the life of the sister they could hear laughing inside as Izel stepped through her feet.

“Would I have made the same choice, if it wasn’t my own sister on the other side of the knife?” Maryam asked the night. “I’m not sure. Most nights, I fear not.”

“You can’t know that,” Angharad quietly said.

“No,” Maryam said. “But then I think about how much easier it is to care about what a black cloak means, when wearing it means I get to have you – all of you. That I get to help the Orels and many more. That I get to live under a roof with people I trust, that I get to learn what I’ve wanted to since I was a girl, get to laugh and drink shitty beer that Old Horvat dug up in port and then sit with you under the stars.”

She folded her arms over her chest.

“And then I think about how that cloak would just be dyed cloth, without all of it,” Maryam confessed. “She’s not the Ecclesiarch, Angharad. She didn’t choose to burn a nation to play god-king. Wei, she made a bad call and followed it down to the bitter end.”

“It doesn’t change what she did,” Angharad said.

“No,” her friend agreed. “But I don’t think she’s a monster, either. Her being an asshole and trying to do you harm doesn’t make her one either. The Machinist isn’t her friend, he’s her owner. And her being an asshole and a deserter who tried to siphon out your life doesn’t mean she’s not also on the wrong side of that thing’s boot.”

Angharad looked up at the sky, eyes chasing the same distant stars.

“No,” she softly said, “I suppose it doesn’t.”

Sometimes, Angharad thought that the most frightful thing about Maryam Khaimov was not her Signs but her compassion. The way it pierced through false faces and anger to get at the bone of things, even when that cast was unkind.

But, Angharad thought as they sat together looking at the stars, sometimes she thought it might be the most admirable thing about her instead.

--

Tristan found that they all visited their own particular ways.

Song was regular and punctual: every day the first week then every other day, usually for around an hour. More if she was bringing him notes and coursework. Angharad went by sentiment, either accompanying another or coming by when she’d thought of something. News she thought he might be interested in, a book they’d discussed, food they both enjoyed. It was regular only in the sense that she never let too long pass without a visit.

Maryam and Ester came together, and the way it went was... mixed. Sometimes they stayed so long they spent the night sleeping in a chair, other times they were gone in a quarter hour. Tristan had thought them sensitive to his moods – he was not always of a mind for company – but he’d eventually come to realize they were chewing on a conversation. Not mustering up courage for it, as he’d thought, but instead holding _back _on having it.

They brought the Orels sometimes. More surprising had been that the Orels sometimes came on their own. Old Horvat thrice, to bring him some pasty vegetable dish he called _duvec_ that was like a chunkier Sacromontan_ pisto_, and Poltava twice to ask questions about from which shops she should try to source the materials for replacement parts she was working in.

Bolic came once, to have a look at him. Up and down, like a man taking the measure of a rival.

“Skinny,” Orel Bolic said.

“Diminishingly useful,” Tristan replied with a pleasant smile.

Bolic did not visit again.

Izel’s visits were in some ways the oddest. Today he’d stumbled in dragging a satchel of small parts and tucked set of tools he’d used to assemble small clockwork mechanisms while talking. _We owe a certain amount for the mechanics assignment and I’m helping Jingyi since he hurt his hand_, Izel had explained. Last time he’d brought paper prints that needed marking for errors, the time before that a full jar of honey he’d not so much dipped bread in so much as outright immersed.

In a way Izel’s visits were the easiest on him, because the tinker was not really here as a visit. He was just company, and there was something soothing about that.

“-and Ester’s a fairly good dancer,” Izel laughed. “Had to hand her off to the little Orel after a few dances, though, that drink had more kick than I’d thought.”

There was a faint click and the tinker yelped, shaking his hand before he sucked at his finger. No blood, Tristan saw, but the skin was red. The gears had ticked the wrong way and pinched him.

“_Dirt-Eater_, that stung,” Izel muttered.

Tristan blinked.

“Dirt-Eater?” he repeated, just to be sure.

“Goddess of forgiveness, among other things,” Izel said. “She takes upon herself the sins and sorrows of others.”

Well, that explained why he’d not really heard of her before. Most Izcalli he had encountered were light on asking for forgiveness. Or permission, for that matter. He leaned forward off the cushions, openly amused.

“So you just tried to pass off the pinching onto that poor goddess?” Tristan asked.

“It is her role to redeem all things into herself,” Izel replied, perhaps a tad defensively.

“And to think we call you the most religious of us,” Tristan tutted, sadly shaking his head.

“You are an actual high priest,” Izel indignantly replied, pointing his wrench like a finger. “How is this even a matter of debate?”

“You might have noticed that Fortuna ran a little thin on the ground, theologically speaking,” Tristan said, and her name wasn’t even enough to wipe out his good mood entirely.

Not so long as he didn’t let himself keep thinking about her.

“I always assumed you held your rites privately,” Izel said. “It is uncommon in Izcalli, but not so elsewhere in Vesper.”

It was difficult to get any less private than painting your patron god’s colors on your face, Tristan conceded.

“I never did much before the shrine,” he said, feeling a pang there. “Though in all fairness I had no idea I was her celebrant for most our time together.”

“And yet you are quite popular with gods,” Izel noted. “Scolomancia took a shine to you as well, insofar as that can be said to be a boon.”

He grimaced.

“It isn’t,” he said, then to his own surprise added more. “She’s trying to elbow out Fortuna.”

Izel breathed in sharply.

“Forgive me, but I was under the impression that after the Lady of Long Odds was imprisoned you lost access to both her and your contract.”

“I did,” Tristan said. “But when she first saved my life, she left something in me.”

He licked his lips.

“And then again, when we fell into the layer together. I don’t know if it was to guide where I fell or more, but it felt... larger, the second time. I sensed it in a way I did not the first. And since then the vultures only got hungrier for it.”

“That is remarkable,” Izel quietly said. “Most gods struggle to achieve anything outside of their immediate domain. I hesitate to call what you describe a boon, either.”

“I don’t think it’s given me anything,” Tristan agreed.

Unless it had not been an accident that Fortuna’s last gift had prevented Scolomancia from simply sinking her claws into him. It _was_ possible, but he doubted it. No one who lost so commandingly often at dice games could have any form of foretelling.

“Then I wonder what it is,” Izel mused. “Because it cannot simply be a blessing of nothing, Tristan. A god is made of a particular aether taint, if they give part of themselves...”

“That taint is still in it,” Tristan muttered. “But I haven’t really gotten anything from it, Izel. No strange thoughts, no instincts, no powers.”

“That is odd,” Izel said. “Although...”

“Although?”

“Perhaps the gift is simply that it is a part of her,” Izel said.

He cocked his head to the side.

“Like she handed me her heart while it still beats?”

“Smaller than a heart, else you would be a Saint by now. But if the part in you is still alive, and she is as well, then that open possibilities. The two parts would still be linked, Tristan.”

His fingers clenched.

“And you think you can do something with that?” he asked.

“Use it for pathfinding, at the very least,” Izel muttered. “Like a compass. And maybe a little more.”

He cleared his throat.

“Have you ever given a blessing before?” the tinker asked. “As a priest, I mean. And I don’t mean mumbling Orthodoxy words either."

"No,” Tristan slowly said.

Izel leaned in.

“Would you like to try?”

Tristan met his eyes.

“You think it will help?”

“I think it cannot hurt,” Izel honestly replied.

His fingers clenched.

“All right,” Tristan whispered. “Let’s try.”

There was a pause.

“I’m going to have to sell so many aether spike dispensers to pay for this,” Izel mourned.

--

Maryam steadied her arm, exhaled to empty her lungs and pulled the trigger. The flint struck and sparked, the powder caught and a heartbeat later the pistol spat out a plume of smoke a shot that...

“Oh, come on,” she complained. “That should have hit the chest.”

The target at the end of the shooting range, a large bale of straw with a person’s silhouette painted on it in red, was sporting a fresh shoulder wound. If it’d been the right shoulder at least Maryam would have understood, she tended to drift rightwards since she’d lost her eye. It was, unfortunately, squarely in the _left_ shoulder.

“I believe the trouble might be with your stance,” Angharad shared. “Song described it as-”

“If I hear Song Ren’s description of the proper shooting stance one more time, I may well go mad,” Maryam warned.

There was a pause.

“Duly noted,” Angharad said, visibly trying not to be too amused.

“Oh, just take your turn,” she groused.

Unforgivably, Angharad actually landed the knee shot that she’d called. It was heinous how quickly she was becoming one of the better shots in the Thirteenth, considering she’d barely ever used guns before enrolling in the Watch. At least Maryam could blame her stalling skills on her dead eye, even though she was keeping it dead on purpose. She felt it safer to practice for the eventuality of Ester being unable to lend an eye, and it wasn’t like practice didn’t help for when she _could_ see properly.

They reloaded together, then fired again. Maryam called and caught a stomach shot, going for the lowest branch in the tree to preserve her pride, while Angharad took the opposite knee.

“You know, it never occurred to me,” Maryam said. “But didn’t your household hunt? I’d expect you to be familiar with fowling guns.”

The caliber of most muskets used in war was likely to pulverize any bird it hit, so hunting guns were usually smaller bores with longer barrels.

“Some of us did,” Angharad said. “Mother was not fond of hunting, but my father’s falconry was widely admired. There are few game birds near Llanw Hall, however, so ours were usually honor hunts – boars, bears and wolves.”

Honor hunts, she mused, were probably the same as_ jezik _hunts. One of the legal obligations of landowners to their tenants across the coastlands: to ride out and slay any beast that damaged kin, crops or livestock then bring back the tongue as proof. All the animals Angharad had named were dangerous to men, and all too willing to attack them.

“A fowling piece won’t do much more than tickle a boar or a bear, unless you get the eye,” Maryam conceded. “And reading between the lines you didn’t use muskets either. Don’t tell me you went a-sabering after bears?”

She painted in her mind the image of Angharad Tredegar facing a large brown bear and granting it a duelist’s salute, that fancy little shoulder tap she liked to do. Alas, the thought could not be as comical as Maryam would have wanted when she’d seen the mirror-dancer kill monsters that large using the weapon in question.

It was still a_ little_ funny, though.

“Maryam, really,” Angharad sighed. “It was done from atop a horse, using hunting spears. Pereduri do not thirst after prize hunts like the Malani do, but we’ve our own traditions.”

“I’ve never seen you use a hunting spear,” Maryam noted.

“The climbing spears we used on the false dantesvara and the ketos are modeled after the Malani standard,” Angharad told her. “Though I confess I take after my mother in this – I never took much joy from the hunt, and learned only as much as I must.”

She cleared her throat.

“Hunting is not as prestigious as it once was, but any noble of good standing is expected to be able to at least ride with a spear in hand,” she said.

Maryam cocked her head to the side.

“What did your mother have against hunting?”

“She was very fond of birds,” Angharad quietly said. “She even forbade commoners to hunt puffins in our lands, since they are seabirds.”

The commoners had probably been less than charmed by that whim, Maryam thought, but she did not feel up to spoiling was what obviously a fond remembrance. Best to change the subject.

“And seabirds are special why?” she asked.

“It is an old superstition,” Angharad admitted, “but it is said that the spirits of slain sea birds will ride storms to come take their revenge on mariners.”

Finally a proper spirit story out of Peredur! The Isles were usually dull in that regard, since the priests of their Sleeping God tended to come down hard on ‘idolaters’.

“So even you monotheists have your superstitions,” she smirked. “Good to know.”

“It is seen as provincial,” her friend replied. “Mother was made fun of in court because of it. A poem was circulated that made Maraire rhyme with a slang word for credulous.”

Maraire? It took Maryam a moment to place the surname.

“Right, because Pereduri nobles need to have a Malani name as well,” Maryam muttered, then cleared her throat. “What’s with the double names, anyhow?”

“The peerage list is the register of the noble bloodlines of the Duchy of Peredur,” Angharad said. “But it is held and penned by the Pereduri themselves, taking no guidance from the royal court.”

“Sounds wise,” Maryam said.

The royal court should be burned and salt sown where it’d stood, as far as she was concerned, but keeping their distance was probably the best the Pereduri could hope for. The strait between Peredur and Malan was a lot shorter a swim than making it all the way to Juska.

“The last duke of Peredur thought so, when he knelt to Queen Perpetual,” Angharad said. “It was one of the boons that let him convince the lords and ladies of the High Isle that peace should be sought. The issue is that for one to obtain further titles, honors or incomes from the crown they must be recognized as noble on Malan’s own rolls of nobility.”

“So why not use the same name for both?” Maryam asked.

It seemed the obvious solution.

“It is forbidden by the crown,” Angharad said. “Else our peers would be recognized as noble by law twice, and thus set above the nobles of Malan and Uthukile. It is largely a formality for one on the peerage list to be recognized in the rolls, though it does require traveling to Isasha in person.”

Maryam hummed. ‘Largely’ a formality meant sometimes it was not, which sounded like a very useful threat for the crown to wield. Back home the Staresine would have never stood for a king having that sort of power, but then there was a reason the Recnigvor word for the royalty across the water translated to ‘tyrant-king’. Crowns in Aurager tended to have a lot more power than they’d ever been allowed to gather in the coastlands.

“It sounds like being on those rolls from the start is an advantage for the Malani,” she said.

“It is,” Angharad darkly said. “Some of the smaller houses must start saving up for the journey to Isasha as soon as their lady grows older, else the unplanned expense of a sudden death could push them into debt. And it is costly in a different way to avoid the journey: any house not on the rolls will be subject to the burden tax as if they were common-born, and often the war tax as well.”

“So why not end the peerage lists outright?” Maryam asked.

More to prod than because she endorsed the solution.

“It would be a decision without pride,” Angharad stiffly said. “A renunciation of our heritage. It is...”

She paused. Maryam raised an eyebrow.

“Well, it is one of the reasons that Nkosinathi Morcant is frowned upon by other Pereduri,” Angharad said. “His first name is already Malani, as if he were trying for the list from birth, and it is said his mother attempted exactly what you described.”

“Getting the Morcant title moved from the peerage list to the nobility rolls,” she said.

Angharad nodded.

“The great families of the duchy would never lower themselves thus,” she said. “But I hear that Lady Morcant is ambitious. Hers was not always considered a powerful house, and she cannot compete in land or blood. I suppose she sees cleaving closer to the royal court as a way to rise.”

“That and the colonies are run by royal governors,” Maryam evenly said. “I expect the crown buys at least half the slaves out of Juska, so she’s putting her allegiance where her wealth flows from.”

“It is grasping of her,” Angharad scorned. “Most of the great families curry some favor with the crown, but none are quite so shameless about it. I am told she sent her sons to attend the isikole in the capital.”

Maryam blinked.

“Nathi Morcant was raised in Isasha?”

“The isikole lasts only four years,” Angharad corrected, “so I would not say raised, exactly. He was clearly meant for court, though. Thando once told me that his departure for the Watch was the subject of much gossip back home.”

“So sending him to the Watch was not the plan from the start.”

Angharad shrugged.

“I will not claim to know the secret thoughts of Lady Morcant,” she said, “but that seems unlikely. The point of the sending her sons to an Isasha isikole should have been to foster ties with other noble scions in those classrooms, and those ties are of little use on Tolomontera.”

“So why_ did_ he get sent here?” Maryam asked.

She chewed at the inside of her cheek a bit.

“Maybe he angered someone from a better family,” she mused. “Or killed someone.”

“His family would not still be supporting him openly had he slain in an unlawful manner,” Angharad said.

“So whatever it is, he left without trashing his reputation first,” Maryam said.

She crossed her arms, pistol resting empty against the crook of her elbow.

“It could have been his contract,” she said. “We’re still not sure what the_ ubunjalo_ he takes from people to fuel his fleshcrafting actually is. Maybe he tried it out and harmed someone without meaning to.”

“That would have been seized on by the Morcant’s enemies and become scandal,” Angharad said. “Or, if the matter was buried, he would now be in the service of the great noble who did the silencing.”

“Then maybe the contract itself is borderline,” Maryam tried. “We know that the Watch sometimes presses into service people with dangerous powers or prices. Normally they get assigned somewhere an eye is kept on them, but since he’s from a powerful family...”

“They leveraged that into Scholomance instead,” Angharad thoughtfully said. “I balk at the notion for the same reason you deem it credible: the Morcant are not nobodies, Maryam. The Watch would find it difficult to take a son of theirs for a contract does not actually break the Iscariot Accords.”

Angharad paused.

“And even should Lady Morcant be heartless, an ambitious woman would not easily throw away a contract as useful as Nathi’s.”

It was arguably even more powerful in Malan, where Maryam suspected few would think twice at feeding the bastard a steady flow of slaves to let him work his craft.

“That’s true,” she muttered. “So whatever got him sent here, it made him unfit for court but without disgracing him. That’s a pretty narrow line to walk.”

Some kind of private disaster, a succession conflict that could be nipped in the bud by placing a black cloak on Nathi’s shoulders?

“I hesitate to wish that Song had read his full contract,” Angharad said, “since it is something of a breach of privacy. And yet.”

Maryam snorted.

“It’s inconvenient she never found out his price,” she agreed. “Mind you, it feels swinish to complain of that when no one else would have the part that she read.”

There’d been few opportunities for Song to get a good read on Morcant contract at the start of the year, when he’d still seemed a lesser threat – their captain couldn’t just stare five minutes above someone’s head in public without outing her own very perilous contract - and by the time he was trouble enough to warrant the effort there had been none. He must have been read in on the suspicions about Song’s contract because he’d very carefully avoided being in her presence for more than small moments. Now he was outright in hiding.

“I knew he’d be a problem,” Maryam said. “But I underestimated how much. What Song suspects, that he’s the one who provided the oil and tar to Cai Wei? It’s a few lines past what I expected from him.”

She’d had him pegged as dangerous and cruel, someone who would keep hounding them until accord was reached, but this was almost manic. If he got caught, the Watch would hang him for it.

“Agreed. He acts like a courtier about to be disgraced,” Angharad absent-mindedly said, beginning to clean and reload her pistol.

Maryam followed suit.

“Meaning?”

Angharad seemed surprised, then thoughtful.

“The royal court in Isasha is not like the Calendar Court or Indulkapur,” Angharad said. “If a courtier is proved to be dishonorable, there is no way _back_. No going into exile and returning, no pilgrimage or flower war to clear one’s name: there can be no blemishes on the honor of the High Queen’s court.”

She tapped the pistol against her shoulder.

“I did not realize it then, as I never attended court myself,” Angharad said. “But as you once pointed out, Nathi followed the traditional methods of a courtier in dealing with us: he offered a private bargain that would make some restitution while ending any notion that he had been in the wrong.”

“I don’t see how arming Cai Wei fits in there,” Maryam pointed out.

Trying to get Izel to kill someone had been a pretty bloody plot to get the Unluckies disbanded – and would have succeeded, if not for Yaotl Acatl – but even if he was caught red-handed it shouldn’t get him worse than expelled.
